pages.title: Socratic Discussion Questions
pages.html:
Socratic Discussion Questions

  1. A Treasury bill sells at $950 and pays $1,000 at maturity. Why does a lower price mean a higher yield, and why does the Treasury yield serve as a benchmark for other interest rates?

  2. Why would anyone accept a lower return? What does a safe investment buy, and what does a risky one charge for the risk?

  3. Fractional-reserve banking lets banks lend most of what is deposited. What do we gain, what do we risk, and what did the banking panics of Module 6 teach about it?

  4. The Fed has two goals, maximum employment and stable prices, and they can pull apart. How would you decide when they conflict, and who bears the cost of the choice?

  5. When the FOMC raises its target range, a family buying a house pays more each month, yet the Fed says it is acting to protect families. Explain both claims.

  6. A fixed rate protects a borrower from future rate increases. What does it not protect against?

  7. In an amortized loan, the early payments are mostly interest. Why is the loan built that way, and who benefits?

  8. A lower rate is not automatically cheaper once closing costs are counted. How would you choose among the same three loan offers for a buyer who will stay four years, seven years, or fifteen years?

  9. What is the tipping point of a loan, and how can a borrower move it? Is paying extra always the wise choice?

  10. “What am I paying for the privilege of borrowing?” How would you answer that for a house, a car, and a credit card, and what should a young person ask before signing any promise to repay?

pages.title: Lesson 8.01 - Reading Quiz
pages.html:
Lesson 8.01 - Reading Quiz

  1. A one-year Treasury bill has a face value of $1,000. An investor pays $950 for it. About what is the yield?

    Answer: B) 5.26 percent

    Why: The investor earns $1,000 minus $950, which is $50. The yield is $50 divided by the $950 paid, about 5.26 percent. Dividing by $1,000 would be the wrong base.

  2. A year after you bought a 10-year note paying 4 percent, new notes are being sold that pay 5 percent. If you want to sell your old note, what will probably happen to its price?

    Answer: B) It will fall, so that the buyer's yield can compete with the new notes

    Why: The payments on the old note are fixed. To compete, its price must fall, and the yield for the person who buys it rises. Price and yield move opposite ways.

  3. A Treasury bill pays interest every six months.

    Answer: False

    Why: A bill pays no regular interest. You buy it for less than face value and receive the full face value at maturity. Notes and bonds pay interest every six months.

  4. Why is the Treasury yield called a benchmark?

    Answer: C) Other lenders start from it and add something for risk

    Why: Treasuries are among the safest investments, backed by the taxing power of the government. Anyone riskier has to offer more.

  5. What problem were TIPS (inflation-protected securities) designed to answer?

    Answer: A) Inflation quietly shrinking what a fixed payment can buy, since the principal rises with the Consumer Price Index

    Why: A saver who cares about buying power, not just dollars, has a reason to look at them.

pages.title: Lesson 8.02 - Reading Quiz
pages.html:
Lesson 8.02 - Reading Quiz

  1. Why does fractional-reserve banking make bank runs possible?

    Answer: B) Banks keep only a fraction as reserves and lend the rest, so they cannot pay everyone at once

    Why: A bank can pay back depositors on a normal day. It cannot pay all of them at once, because most of the money is out in loans.

  2. In the textbook story, banks keep a fixed fraction of each deposit as reserves. If that fraction were 20 percent, the most a $1,000 deposit could support in total deposits is:

    Answer: C) $5,000

    Why: $1,000 divided by 0.20 is $5,000. A higher reserve ratio holds back more of each deposit, so the total is lower.

  3. As of March 26, 2020, the Federal Reserve Board set reserve requirement ratios at zero percent.

    Answer: True

    Why: The Board said this followed "the shift to an ample reserves regime." Banks are still limited by capital rules, by the need to find borrowers who will repay, and by the cost of lending that the Fed's rate decisions change.

  4. Which two tools does the lesson say do most of the Fed's work today?

    Answer: B) Open market operations and the interest the Fed pays banks on reserves

    Why: A bank has little reason to lend reserves to another bank for less than the Fed pays it to leave them there, so that rate acts as a floor.

  5. What does the Federal Open Market Committee vote on?

    Answer: B) A target range for the federal funds rate

    Why: The Fed then uses its tools to keep the actual rate inside that range. The rate ripples out to other rates.

pages.title: Lesson 8.02 - Primary Source Exercise
pages.html:
Lesson 8.02 - Primary Source Exercise

"In support of these goals, the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent and anticipates that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate."

"Inflation remains elevated, reflecting supply and demand imbalances related to the pandemic, higher energy prices, and broader price pressures."

Federal Reserve, "Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement," March 16, 2022. federalreserve.gov.

  1. What did the Committee decide to do?

    Answer: C) Raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent

    Why: This ended a period, since March 2020, in which the range had been held near zero.

  2. The statement also says the Committee "anticipates that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate." Why does that signal matter?

    Answer: B) It shapes what banks and borrowers expect and do before anything else happens

    Why: People adjust to what they expect the Fed to do, so the forecast itself changes behavior.

  3. Which cause of elevated inflation does the statement name?

    Answer: B) Higher energy prices

    Why: The statement lists supply and demand imbalances related to the pandemic, higher energy prices, and broader price pressures.

  4. James Bullard dissented, preferring a 0.5 percentage point increase to a range of 1/2 to 3/4 percent. Compared with what the Committee chose, his preference would have been:

    Answer: C) A larger and faster increase in rates

    Why: He did not oppose raising rates. He wanted a bigger step. Even the experts disagreed about how fast to go.

pages.title: Lesson 8.03 - Reading Quiz
pages.html:
Lesson 8.03 - Reading Quiz

  1. On the sample $162,000 loan at 3.875 percent, the first monthly payment is $761.78. About how much of that first payment is interest?

    Answer: B) $523.13

    Why: Interest is charged on the full balance: $162,000 times the monthly rate 0.0032292 is about $523.13. The remaining $238.65 reduces the principal.

  2. Which factor that sets your rate is controlled by markets and the Fed, not by you?

    Answer: A) The benchmark rate

    Why: You cannot control the benchmark, but you can control a lot of what is added to it.

  3. The annual percentage rate (APR) on a loan is always the same as its interest rate.

    Answer: False

    Why: The APR folds in the loan's fees and other costs. On the sample form, the interest rate is 3.875 percent and the APR is 4.274 percent.

  4. What is an escrow account?

    Answer: B) An account where the lender holds part of your payment to pay your property taxes and homeowner's insurance

    Why: In the sample, escrow is $206 a month. It protects the lender, since an unpaid tax bill can put a claim on the house.

  5. Whom does private mortgage insurance protect?

    Answer: C) The lender, if the borrower stops paying

    Why: Lenders often require it when the down payment is small. In the sample it adds $82 a month for the first seven years.

pages.title: Lesson 8.03 - Primary Source Exercise
pages.html:
Lesson 8.03 - Primary Source Exercise

"Annual Percentage Rate (APR) 4.274%. Your costs over the loan term expressed as a rate. This is not your interest rate."

"In 5 Years: $56,582. Total you will have paid in principal, interest, mortgage insurance, and loan costs. $15,773. Principal you will have paid off."

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, sample Loan Estimate H-24(B), Fixed Rate Loan, February 7, 2014 (page 3, "Comparisons"). The names and lender on the sample are fictional.

  1. The sample's interest rate is 3.875 percent, and its APR is 4.274 percent. Why is the APR higher?

    Answer: B) The APR expresses the loan's costs over its term as a rate, so it includes fees as well as interest

    Why: The form says so in one sentence: the APR is "not your interest rate."

  2. Roughly what share of the $56,582 paid over five years went to reduce principal?

    Answer: B) About 28 percent

    Why: $15,773 divided by $56,582 is about 0.279, or about 28 percent. The rest went to interest, mortgage insurance, and loan costs.

  3. Suppose two lenders offer the same loan, and one has a lower interest rate but a much higher APR. What should a careful borrower conclude?

    Answer: B) The lower-rate lender probably charges higher fees, so the other loan may cost less overall, and the borrower should ask why

    Why: If one lender has a lower rate and a much higher APR, ask why. A careful borrower asks until the answers make sense.

  4. Why did so little of the five-year total go to principal?

    Answer: C) Early payments on an amortized loan are mostly interest, and the total also includes mortgage insurance and loan costs

    Why: Interest is charged on the balance you still owe, so it is largest at the beginning.

pages.title: Lesson 8.04 - Reading Quiz
pages.html:
Lesson 8.04 - Reading Quiz

  1. On the sample loan, the tipping point comes at payment number 147. What does that mean?

    Answer: C) It is the first payment in which more than half goes to principal

    Why: In payment 146, interest is still ahead by two cents. In payment 147, principal is ahead: $382.11 against $379.67. That is 12 years and 3 months into the loan.

  2. After five years of payments on the $162,000 loan, about how much of the original loan is still owed?

    Answer: A) About 90 percent

    Why: The balance after 60 payments is $146,227.42, about 90.3 percent of $162,000. If you sell after five years, the sale price has to cover that before you keep any profit.

  3. Compared with the 30-year loan at the same rate, a 15-year loan has:

    Answer: B) A higher payment and much lower total interest

    Why: The monthly payment goes from $761.78 to $1,188.17, but total interest falls from $112,240.80 to $51,870.60. You owe the balance for fewer months.

  4. A refinance costs $2,400 and lowers the monthly payment by $40. How many months does it take to break even?

    Answer: C) 60 months

    Why: Divide the cost by the monthly savings: $2,400 divided by $40 is 60 months. If you expect to move or pay off the loan sooner, you lose money by refinancing.

  5. What does the total cost of credit include?

    Answer: B) Interest plus required fees and insurance, not the amount borrowed

    Why: Decide what belongs by asking: would I pay this if I did not need to borrow?

pages.title: Module 8 - Test
pages.html:
Module 8 - Test

  1. A one-year Treasury bill with a $1,000 face value sells for $940. What is the approximate yield?

    Answer: C) 6.38 percent

    Why: $1,000 minus $940 is $60, and $60 divided by $940 is about 6.38 percent.

  2. If investors suddenly want the safety of Treasury securities and bid up their price, what happens to yields?

    Answer: A) They fall

    Why: The payoff at maturity is fixed, so a higher price means a lower return on the money you put in.

  3. Which statement describes the relationship between a Treasury yield and a bank's mortgage rate?

    Answer: B) Lenders start from the benchmark yield for a similar maturity and add a premium for risk

    Why: Mortgage rates and long-term Treasury yields tend to move in the same direction over time.

  4. A lender builds a rate this way: a 4.0 percent benchmark, plus 0.5 percentage points for the long term, plus 1.0 percentage point for the borrower's late payments. What rate does it ask?

    Answer: B) 5.5 percent

    Why: 4.0 plus 0.5 plus 1.0 is 5.5 percent. A borrower with a spotless history would see the credit add-on shrink or disappear.

  5. Which borrower is likely to pay the highest rate, according to the lesson's risk ladder?

    Answer: D) A borrower with weak credit

    Why: Risk rises along the ladder, and so does the rate a lender asks, because repayment is least certain for the weak-credit borrower.

  6. When the government runs a deficit, how does it cover the gap?

    Answer: B) By selling Treasury securities, which are auctioned to investors

    Why: The price is set by buyers and sellers, not by a government order. Over time the interest on this borrowing becomes a cost in the budget.

  7. Which type of Treasury security pays interest every six months and returns face value in 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years?

    Answer: B) Treasury note

    Why: Bills run 4 to 52 weeks and pay no regular interest. Bonds run 20 or 30 years.

  8. With a reserve ratio of 10 percent, what is the most that a $1,000 deposit can support in total deposits?

    Answer: D) $10,000

    Why: $1,000 divided by 0.10 is $10,000. Lending creates money: the new deposits are real spending power that did not exist before the loans.

  9. Since March 26, 2020, what has been the required reserve ratio set by the Federal Reserve Board?

    Answer: A) Zero percent

    Why: The textbook multiplier story still shows how lending creates deposits, but it is no longer the rule that limits banks.

  10. What does the Fed's dual mandate consist of?

    Answer: B) Maximum employment and stable prices

    Why: The two goals can pull against each other. Lower rates help employment but can push prices up, and higher rates cool prices but can slow hiring.

  11. Which sequence correctly traces how an FOMC rate increase reaches borrowers?

    Answer: B) The target range rises, banks pay more for short-term money, banks raise loan rates, borrowing costs more, spending cools

    Why: A rate decision that looks small in the news is large when multiplied across a lifetime of borrowing.

  12. On a $162,000 30-year loan, the monthly payment rises from $761.78 at 3.875 percent to $857.32 at 4.875 percent. About how much does one percentage point add each month?

    Answer: B) About $95

    Why: $857.32 minus $761.78 is $95.54. Over 360 months that is tens of thousands of dollars.

  13. Why do variable-rate loans respond quickly when the Fed changes course?

    Answer: C) Their rates move up and down with a benchmark

    Why: A fixed-rate loan locks in the rate you were given. Fixed rates are usually a little higher at the start in exchange for certainty.

  14. A borrower takes a $200,000 loan at 6 percent for 30 years. The monthly payment is $1,199.10. How much of the first payment is interest?

    Answer: B) $1,000.00

    Why: The monthly rate is 0.06 divided by 12, or 0.005. Interest is $200,000 times 0.005, or $1,000.00. The other $199.10 reduces the principal.

  15. For that same $200,000 loan, which is closest to the total interest paid over 30 years?

    Answer: C) About $231,700

    Why: 360 payments of $1,199.10 total $431,676. Subtract the $200,000 borrowed, and the interest is about $231,700. Total payments are about 2.16 times what was borrowed.

  16. Why does the interest part of each payment shrink over time on an amortized loan?

    Answer: B) Interest is charged on the balance still owed, which gets smaller

    Why: The payment is fixed, so as interest shrinks, the part left over for principal grows. Early payments are mostly interest.

  17. Which statement about credit scores is supported by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, as quoted in the lesson?

    Answer: C) Most scores run from 300 to 850, and you do not have just one score, since it can vary by model, by kind of loan, and by date

    Why: The Bureau calls a score "a prediction of your credit behavior."

  18. In the sample Loan Estimate, the home costs $180,000 and the loan is $162,000. What percent is the down payment?

    Answer: B) 10 percent

    Why: The down payment is $18,000, which is 10 percent of $180,000. A bigger down payment lowers the lender's risk.

  19. How is the sample's "Estimated Cash to Close" of $16,054 built?

    Answer: B) Closing costs of $8,054 plus the $18,000 down payment, minus the $10,000 deposit already paid

    Why: $8,054 plus $18,000 is $26,054, minus $10,000 is $16,054. Closing costs are often forgotten when families plan a purchase.

  20. In the sample, the projected monthly payment falls from $1,050 in years 1 to 7 to $968 in years 8 to 30. Why?

    Answer: D) The mortgage insurance of $82 a month ends

    Why: $1,050 minus $82 is $968. Principal and interest ($761.78) and escrow ($206) continue.

  21. The Total Interest Percentage on the sample form (69.45 percent) differs slightly from a straight calculation of total interest divided by the loan amount (about 69.3 percent). What does the lesson recommend?

    Answer: C) Report the small gap honestly, and use that line only to compare loans on the same form

    Why: When two honest numbers disagree slightly, say so and keep working, rather than pretending they match.

  22. A student compares a 48-month and a 60-month car loan for $20,000 at 6 percent. The 48-month total interest is $2,545.60, and the 60-month total is $3,199.60. How much more interest does the longer loan cost?

    Answer: C) $654.00

    Why: $3,199.60 minus $2,545.60 is $654.00. The longer loan is easier on the monthly budget but keeps her in debt another year while the car loses value.

  23. Why are extra payments especially powerful early in a loan?

    Answer: B) They reduce the principal while it is large, so less interest builds up afterward

    Why: Adding $100 to every payment on the sample loan pays it off in 290 months instead of 360, saving about $24,576 in interest. Check for a prepayment penalty first.

  24. The sample loan's total cost of credit comes to about $124,801. Which items add up to it?

    Answer: B) Interest of $112,240.80, loan costs of $5,672, and mortgage insurance of $6,888 (82 times 84)

    Why: Taxes and homeowner's insurance are real costs but not costs of credit. The test is: would I pay this if I did not need to borrow?

  25. Which step in the seven-step credit plan helps protect you if your income falls or a variable rate rises?

    Answer: D) Risks

    Why: The steps are purpose, price and down payment, rate, term, total cost of credit, budget, and risks. They do not guarantee a good result, but they make a bad surprise far less likely.

pages.title: Module 8 - Quarter 2 Exam
pages.html:
Module 8 - Quarter 2 Exam

Teacher-facing: the bracketed codes are lesson and CPALMS benchmark references. Answers shuffle in Canvas, so use the answer text, not the letter.

  1. [5.01, E.3.2] In one day, Country X can produce either 6 cars or 12 televisions, and Country Y can produce either 2 cars or 8 televisions. Which statement is correct?

    Answer: B) Country X has the comparative advantage in cars, and Country Y has the comparative advantage in televisions

    Why: Country X gives up 2 televisions per car, and Country Y gives up 4. X has the lower opportunity cost of cars. Y gives up only 0.25 car per television, against 0.5 for X, so Y has the comparative advantage in televisions, even though X produces more of both.

  2. [5.01, E.3.2] Why can a country gain from trade even if it has no absolute advantage in anything?

    Answer: B) It can specialize where its opportunity cost is lowest, and both countries end up with more

    Why: Comparative advantage means being the "least bad" at something relative to your own alternatives.

  3. [5.02, E.3.3] An importer pays a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on a $200 imported good. How much is the tariff?

    Answer: C) $20

    Why: Ad valorem means "according to value": 10 percent of $200 is $20. A specific tariff is a flat dollar amount per unit.

  4. [5.02, E.3.3] A country restricts imports of medical supplies so it never depends on a rival for them. Which rationale for trade barriers is this?

    Answer: B) National security

    Why: National security (oil, food, medical supplies) and foreign policy (sanctions, embargoes) are rationales alongside protecting infant industries.

  5. [5.03, E.2.12] In the circular flow model, where do firms get the land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship they use to produce?

    Answer: B) The factor market, from households

    Why: Households supply the factors of production and earn wages, rent, interest, and profit. They then spend that income in the product market.

  6. [5.04, E.3.5 and HC.11.4] Why does the lesson call the Korean peninsula the clearest "natural experiment"?

    Answer: B) They started in 1945 with the same population, culture, and history, so the later gap isolates the effect of economic and legal systems

    Why: Because almost everything else started out the same, the comparison isolates institutions and property rights.

  7. [5.04, E.3.5] What is "Dutch disease"?

    Answer: C) A commodity boom that raises a currency's value and harms a country's other industries

    Why: Resource-rich developing nations can face it, which is why resource wealth does not guarantee growth.

  8. [5.05, E.3.6] Adam Smith's pin factory illustrates which idea?

    Answer: B) Specialization multiplies productivity

    Why: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Smith also described people pursuing self-interest through markets and serving society's needs too.

  9. [5.05, E.3.6] Which school argued that wages and prices are "sticky" and slow to adjust, leaving real room for policy to matter?

    Answer: C) New Keynesian

    Why: The new classical school stressed rational expectations. New Keynesians stressed stickiness.

  10. [6.01, E.1.12] The lesson calls installment credit a tool, not a wicked thing. What rule does the tool have built in?

    Answer: B) Every payment owed next year comes out of next year's income, and if that income stops, the payments do not

    Why: In the 1920s millions of households took on payments at once, and nobody had tested what would happen if paychecks shrank.

  11. [6.01, HC.11.4] Machines let one farmer plow more land, and more wheat reached the market, so wheat prices fell. What did farmers do next, according to the lesson?

    Answer: B) Plowed even more land to earn the same income, so the native grass that held the soil was lost

    Why: Every single decision made sense. Together they stripped the Plains of its grass.

  12. [6.02, E.1.11] Why did the closing of the Bank of United States in December 1930 matter?

    Answer: B) It was the fourth-largest bank in New York City, and its closing shook trust in banks across the country

    Why: Fear spread faster than facts, and depositors began to worry even about banks that were perfectly healthy.

  13. [6.02, E.2.7] The Dow closed at 41.22 on July 8, 1932. About how far below its September 1929 peak of 381.17 was that?

    Answer: D) About 89 percent

    Why: 41.22 divided by 381.17 is about 0.108, so the Dow was about 89 percent below its peak. A person who put $1,000 into the average stock in September 1929 would have had roughly $110 by the summer of 1932.

  14. [6.03, E.1.12] What is a "discouraged worker"?

    Answer: B) A person who is out of work and has stopped looking, so is not counted as unemployed

    Why: In a deep downturn some people stop looking because there is nothing to find, so even a careful count can miss part of the damage.

  15. [6.03, E.1.12] In the spiral described in Lesson 6.03, what comes right after businesses cut costs because falling prices squeeze profits?

    Answer: B) More workers are laid off, which cuts spending again

    Why: Then the loop starts again from the top, which is why economists fear a steady fall in prices.

  16. [6.04, HC.11.4] The Soil Conservation Service created in 1935 exists today under which name?

    Answer: B) The Natural Resources Conservation Service

    Why: Congress adopted the new name in 1994.

  17. [6.04, HC.11.4] The lesson describes a "sunk-cost trap" for a farm family deciding whether to leave. What is it?

    Answer: A) The more you have already put into a farm, the harder it feels to walk away, though money already spent is gone either way

    Why: A good decision looks forward. That is easy to say and very hard to do.

  18. [6.05, E.1.10 and E.2.9] Why does the lesson say Hoover was "following the textbook of his day"?

    Answer: B) A balanced budget, even in hard times, was widely held as sound policy in 1932, and Keynes's major book arguing the opposite did not appear until 1936

    Why: Whether the textbook was right is what the Depression put to the test.

  19. [6.05, E.1.11] When did the FDIC begin insuring deposits, and for how much per depositor at the start?

    Answer: B) January 1, 1934, up to $2,500, raised to $5,000 in July 1934

    Why: The Banking Act of 1933, often called Glass-Steagall, created the FDIC.

  20. [6.06, E.2.4] On what ground did the Supreme Court hold part of the NIRA unconstitutional in Schechter (1935)?

    Answer: B) It gave too much lawmaking power to the executive branch, and Congress lacked authority over a small local business

    Why: The vote was unanimous, and Chief Justice Hughes wrote the opinion.

  21. [6.06, E.1.12] What does the lesson conclude about the cause of the 1937 recession?

    Answer: B) It is still debated: one argument blames the Fed's doubling of reserve requirements, while other economists found the new rules did not bind most banks

    Why: The cause is not settled. The lesson asks you to be confident of what is documented and honest about what is not.

  22. [7.01, E.3.6] "Resolved personal worth into exchange value." What does the Manifesto mean by this charge against the bourgeoisie?

    Answer: B) Everything, including a worker's time and effort, was reduced to a price

    Why: The authors admired the bourgeoisie's productive power, but they charged that workers did not share in what the machines produced.

  23. [7.01, E.1.3] The Manifesto's measures 7, 8, and 9 (state-owned factories and a common plan, required work and labor armies, and combining farming with manufacturing) are mainly examples of which kind of change?

    Answer: D) Planning

    Why: The lesson sorts the ten measures into ownership of capital, taxation, money and banking, planning, and education. The pattern is that a central authority takes decisions that markets normally make.

  24. [7.02, E.1.3] Which description of Russia in 1917 matches the lesson?

    Answer: B) A mostly farming country, with large factories only in cities such as Petrograd and Moscow

    Why: A strict reading of the Manifesto would have told Lenin to wait. He argued that a small, disciplined party could lead city workers and win farmers' support.

  25. [7.02, E.1.3] After taking power, which actions did the Bolsheviks take in their first months?

    Answer: B) They created the Cheka (secret police) and broke up the elected assembly after a single meeting

    Why: They made peace with Germany in March 1918, and then a civil war began between the Reds and the Whites.

  26. [7.03, E.1.3] Why were Soviet planners' reports on output often unreliable?

    Answer: B) The people who ran the system also reported on it, so numbers could reflect what the system wanted to hear

    Why: Historians describe 1930 as an era of exaggeration in the official claims.

  27. [7.03, E.1.3] What was the lesson's balanced judgment of the Five-Year Plan?

    Answer: C) The industrial base it built helped the Soviet Union survive the 1941 German invasion, but consumer goods fell sharply and food grew scarce

    Why: On the first-order economic problem, producing and distributing enough that the whole population prospers, the record is poor.

  28. [7.04, E.1.3 and E.3.6] Why does the lesson call a price "a message"?

    Answer: B) A price carries knowledge from people who have it to people who need it, without telling them why

    Why: The buyer in the tin example only needs to see that the price has risen.

  29. [7.04, E.1.3] Which pair appears among the causes of the Soviet collapse that historians cite in the lesson?

    Answer: B) The cost of the arms race and a long war in Afghanistan, together with falling oil prices in the 1980s

    Why: Historians do not agree on a single cause. National feeling in the republics and particular decisions also appear.

  30. [7.04, HC.11.4] The lesson adds that much of the Korean peninsula's heavy industry sat in the north in 1945. What does that fact do to the comparison of the two Koreas?

    Answer: B) It makes the gap more striking, because the north started with the advantage

    Why: The lesson still cautions that North Korea's figure is an estimate and that one comparison cannot prove a rule.

  31. [8.01, E.1.15] A one-year Treasury bill with a $1,000 face value sells for $970. About what is the yield?

    Answer: B) 3.09 percent

    Why: $1,000 minus $970 is $30, and $30 divided by $970 is about 3.09 percent. Dividing by the face value would give 3.00 percent, which is the wrong base.

  32. [8.01, E.1.15] An offer promises a high return with no risk. According to the lesson, how should you react?

    Answer: B) With suspicion, because return and risk travel together

    Why: Honesty about this tradeoff is a mark of a trustworthy adviser, and of a trustworthy person managing their own money.

  33. [8.02, E.1.13 and E.2.10] Why does the lesson say the textbook reserve-multiplier story is no longer the rule that limits bank lending?

    Answer: B) The required reserve ratio has been zero since March 26, 2020, so capital rules, finding borrowers who will repay, and the cost of lending now do more of the limiting

    Why: The story still shows how lending creates deposits.

  34. [8.02, E.2.10] Why does the interest the Fed pays on reserves act as a floor under short-term rates?

    Answer: C) A bank has little reason to lend reserves to another bank for less than the Fed pays it to leave them there

    Why: When the Fed raises that rate, other short-term rates tend to follow.

  35. [8.02, E.1.11] A $162,000, 30-year loan costs $672.13 a month at 2.875 percent and $958.29 at 5.875 percent. How much more is the monthly payment at the higher rate?

    Answer: C) $286.16

    Why: $958.29 minus $672.13 is $286.16 a month, across 360 months more than $100,000.

  36. [8.03, E.1.14] On the Loan Estimate, "Balloon Payment: No" means:

    Answer: B) There is no large lump-sum payment due at the end of the loan

    Why: A balloon payment is a large lump sum due at maturity.

  37. [8.03, E.1.14] The sample form's prepayment penalty is "as high as $3,240" in the first two years on a $162,000 loan. What does the lesson say that is?

    Answer: C) 2 percent of the balance for two years

    Why: Two percent of $162,000 is $3,240. A borrower should know exactly what the lender counts as a penalty before sending extra money.

  38. [8.03, E.1.16] How does the lesson say to use the Loan Estimate when shopping?

    Answer: B) Get Loan Estimates for the same loan from at least two lenders, and compare the rate, APR, monthly payment, cash to close, and any penalty side by side

    Why: If one lender has a lower rate and a much higher APR, ask why.

  39. [8.04, E.1.16] The sample loan with 20 percent down ($36,000 down, $144,000 borrowed) has a payment of $677.14. How much less is that per month than the base case of $761.78?

    Answer: B) $84.64

    Why: $761.78 minus $677.14 is $84.64. Total interest also falls, from $112,240.80 to $99,770.40.

  40. [8.04, E.1.16] A refinance costs $4,500 and lowers the monthly payment by $75. How many months does it take to break even?

    Answer: C) 60 months

    Why: $4,500 divided by $75 is 60 months. If you expect to move or pay off the loan sooner, refinancing loses money.

pages.title: Module 8 - Final Exam
pages.html:
Module 8 - Final Exam

Teacher-facing: the bracketed codes are lesson and CPALMS benchmark references. Answers shuffle in Canvas, so use the answer text, not the letter.

  1. [1.01, E.2.1] Tickets to a popular concert sell out in minutes because far more people want them than there are seats. Which idea does this illustrate?

    Answer: A) Scarcity

    Why: Scarcity means there is never enough of everything to satisfy every possible use for it. It is a microeconomic example, since it concerns one market.

  2. [1.02, E.1.2] Two classmates face the same choice, a concert ticket or saving for a phone, and rationally choose differently. Why?

    Answer: C) They place different utility on each option

    Why: Utility is the satisfaction a person gets from a good, service, or choice. Cost-benefit analysis weighs what is gained against what is lost.

  3. [1.03, E.1.1] The lesson calls land a "gift of nature." Which statement is also true of land?

    Answer: C) It is finite and unevenly distributed

    Why: Land covers every natural resource from the Earth: soil, forests, minerals, fossil fuels, sunlight, wind, and water.

  4. [1.04, E.1.3] Which features describe a traditional economy?

    Answer: C) Custom passed down through generations, subsistence production, and barter

    Why: It is the oldest system. It offers strong social cohesion, but little technological change.

  5. [2.01, E.1.4] Which event shifts the supply curve for a good to the right?

    Answer: C) New technology that lowers production costs

    Why: New technology means more at every price. A drought or a new tax shifts supply left, and a rise in income shifts demand right.

  6. [2.02, E.1.6] Why is a firm in perfect competition called a "price taker"?

    Answer: B) There are many small firms selling an identical product, so no single firm can influence the price

    Why: Free entry and exit push long-run economic profit toward zero.

  7. [2.03, E.1.8] What risk does the lesson attach to relying on price competition alone?

    Answer: B) It compresses profit margins and can push firms toward under-investment in quality or workers

    Why: Nonprice competition builds loyalty that survives a price increase, but it requires sustained investment.

  8. [2.04, E.1.5] What is "double taxation" of a corporation?

    Answer: C) The corporation pays tax on its profits, and shareholders pay tax again on the dividends

    Why: An LLC, a pass-through entity, avoids it.

  9. [2.05, E.1.7] An airline's marginal cost for one more passenger on a flight already scheduled is very low. What does that explain?

    Answer: A) Why last-minute discount fares can still be profitable

    Why: Fuel and crew are already paid for, so the extra passenger adds little cost.

  10. [3.01, E.1.13] Zimbabwe and Venezuela both suffered hyperinflation. Which characteristic of good money broke down?

    Answer: B) Limited supply

    Why: Unlimited money collapses in value.

  11. [3.02, E.1.11] Why do Federal Reserve decisions reverberate around the world?

    Answer: B) The dollar is the world's primary reserve currency, so higher U.S. rates strengthen the dollar and raise repayment costs for countries with dollar debt

    Why: The Fed's mandate is officially domestic, but its reach is de facto global.

  12. [3.02, E.2.10] What did the "taper tantrum" refer to?

    Answer: C) Capital that had flowed into emerging markets rushing back to the United States when the Fed raised rates after a period of low rates

    Why: Such shifts can trigger balance-of-payments crises that require help from the International Monetary Fund.

  13. [3.03, E.1.15] Why would a saver choose a Certificate of Deposit over a regular savings account?

    Answer: C) A CD pays a slightly higher rate in exchange for locking funds up for a set term

    Why: CDs trade liquidity for a higher rate.

  14. [3.04, E.1.16] Financial experts generally recommend keeping total monthly debt payments below what share of income?

    Answer: C) 36 percent

    Why: This is a guideline for borrowing within your means. A budget also has to be reviewed monthly, not just built once.

  15. [4.01, E.1.10] Which are the three goals of fiscal policy in the lesson?

    Answer: B) Price stability, full employment, and sustainable growth

    Why: The trade-off across all three is public debt.

  16. [4.02, E.2.9] What is "crowding out"?

    Answer: C) Heavy government borrowing raising interest rates by competing with households and businesses for credit

    Why: Crowding out can make mortgages and business loans more expensive.

  17. [4.03, E.2.7] What happened in Weimar Germany in the 1920s, according to the lesson?

    Answer: B) Prices doubled every few days, savings evaporated, and people resorted to barter or foreign currency

    Why: This is hyperinflation, a different order of magnitude from high inflation.

  18. [4.04, E.2.11] What is a Pigovian tax?

    Answer: B) A tax on an activity that creates a negative externality, meant to make the producer pay something closer to the true social cost

    Why: Cap-and-trade systems and carbon taxes work on a similar principle.

  19. [4.04, E.2.11] Why does the lesson call education a positive externality?

    Answer: C) An educated population raises innovation and civic participation well beyond any individual graduate

    Why: That is the economic case for public investment in schools.

  20. [5.01, E.3.2] Country P can make 20 shirts or 10 phones per day. Country Q can make 10 shirts or 8 phones per day. Which statement is correct?

    Answer: B) Country Q has the comparative advantage in phones, even though P has an absolute advantage in both goods

    Why: P gives up 2 shirts per phone, and Q gives up 1.25. Q has the lower opportunity cost of phones.

  21. [5.02, E.3.3] The USMCA replaced NAFTA. Which countries are its members?

    Answer: A) The United States, Mexico, and Canada

    Why: It is a trade agreement, and it is a shallower form of integration than the European Union.

  22. [5.03, E.2.12] What is the purpose of transfer payments such as unemployment insurance in the circular flow?

    Answer: B) To support households whose private income falls short

    Why: They are not payment for land, labor, or capital.

  23. [5.04, E.3.5] What do Bangladesh and Rwanda show?

    Answer: B) Real economic progress is possible even without abundant natural resources

    Why: The lesson cites Bangladesh's export industries and Rwanda's governance reform.

  24. [5.05, E.3.6] What is stagflation, and why did it challenge the prevailing schools?

    Answer: B) High unemployment and high inflation at once, which neither Keynesians nor monetarists could fix together

    Why: The 1970s embarrassed both schools and pushed the new classical, New Keynesian, and Austrian schools forward.

  25. [6.01, E.1.12] The lesson says a weakening of habits of prudence across a society leaves less room to absorb a shock. How does it treat the claim that this was the main cause of the Depression?

    Answer: C) It says economists still argue about it, and it returns to the debate honestly in Lesson 6.06

    Why: A farmer who borrowed to feed his family was not a speculator. The point is about habits across a whole society.

  26. [6.02, E.2.7] The Federal Reserve's own history reports that the Dow closed at 381.17 on September 3, 1929. According to the lesson, the Dow did not climb back to that high until:

    Answer: C) November 23, 1954

    Why: It reached a low of 41.22 on July 8, 1932.

  27. [6.03, E.1.12] Which place did the lesson use as an example of unemployment reaching 35.8 percent, showing that national figures hide differences?

    Answer: C) Utah

    Why: A town that depended on one mine or one factory could lose nearly everything at once.

  28. [6.04, HC.11.4] Why was the effect of the drought on Plains soil so severe, according to the lesson?

    Answer: B) Plowing had removed the native grass whose roots held the soil, so when the drought came the wind could lift the topsoil

    Why: The prairie had survived dry years for thousands of years. What changed was what lay on top of the ground.

  29. [6.05, E.2.4] Section 7(a) of the National Industrial Recovery Act gave workers the right to:

    Answer: C) Join unions and take part in collective bargaining

    Why: Collective bargaining means bargaining as a group with the employer.

  30. [6.06, E.1.12] Which caution does the lesson attach to Christina Romer's finding that monetary expansion explains nearly all recovery before 1942?

    Answer: B) It is one economist's analysis and does not mean spending did nothing, and critics argue the usual measures may understate fiscal effects

    Why: The lesson does not ask you to choose a winner. It shows how a careful person holds an open question.

  31. [7.01, E.3.6] In "the history of all hitherto existing society," what does "hitherto" mean?

    Answer: C) Up to now

    Why: The authors claim that if you look at any society in recorded history, you will find groups pulling against each other.

  32. [7.02, E.1.3] Why did Lenin's party gain from the provisional government's decision to stay in the war?

    Answer: A) Soldiers and city workers wanted peace and bread, and the government could not provide either

    Why: The Bolsheviks promised "Peace, land, and bread."

  33. [7.03, E.1.3] Why did Stalin's plan put heavy industry first?

    Answer: B) The reasoning was that an industrial base would make the country strong, fast, and the cost was a sharp fall in consumer goods

    Why: Heavy industry means steel, coal, electric power, and machines.

  34. [7.04, E.1.3] Why are GDP-per-person figures for the two Koreas given in "2011 international dollars"?

    Answer: B) The unit adjusts for what money can actually buy in each place

    Why: Per person means the total output divided by the population.

  35. [7.04, E.1.3] A planner might say that modern computers solve the knowledge problem. How does the lesson treat that claim?

    Answer: C) It says economists disagree: some argue the problem is smaller now, while others argue the most useful knowledge is local, changing, and often unspoken

    Why: The lesson asks you to be ready to defend whichever side you find stronger.

  36. [8.01, E.1.15] How is the price of a Treasury security set when it is sold?

    Answer: C) By buyers and sellers, through public auctions where investors bid

    Why: Households, banks, pension funds, and foreign investors all buy them.

  37. [8.02, E.2.10] What does the phrase "ample reserves regime" in the Fed's 2020 announcement mean?

    Answer: A) The banking system holds so many reserves that the Fed steers rates with the interest it pays, not by limiting how many reserves exist

    Why: The reserve requirement ratios were reduced to zero percent, effective March 26, 2020.

  38. [8.03, E.1.14] What is amortization?

    Answer: B) Paying a loan off gradually in equal payments, each covering interest and also reducing the amount owed

    Why: The payment stays the same, but the split between interest and principal changes every month.

  39. [8.03, E.1.14] Which item does the lesson list as something credit scoring models look at?

    Answer: C) How much of your available credit you are using

    Why: The Bureau's list includes your record of paying bills, how much debt you carry, how long accounts have been open, credit use, and recent applications.

  40. [8.04, E.1.16] A family can refinance for $3,000 and cut its payment by $60 a month, but expects to move in three years. What does the break-even test suggest?

    Answer: B) Do not refinance, because 50 months are needed to earn back the cost and they will leave sooner

    Why: $3,000 divided by $60 is 50 months. If you expect to move or pay off the loan sooner, you lose money by refinancing.

Module 8 assignments and project: teacher key

All figures were recomputed from the standard loan formula (script run 2026-10-23). The key workbook's formulas were evaluated with a spreadsheet-formula library and the results matched; they have not been opened in Excel itself. Total interest by the lessons' method is payments times months minus principal. The sum of a schedule's interest column runs a few dollars higher because payments are rounded to the cent (see 8.03).

Scoring modes. Lessons 8.01 and 8.02 are completion-scored (10 points: complete, 5: partly complete, 0: not submitted or off topic). Lessons 8.03 and 8.04 and the Module Project use the rubrics in their descriptions.

8.01 - Pricing the Promise (completion)

Part 1 key (one-year bill, $1,000 face value):

Price paidEarnedYield
$975$252.56% (25 / 975 = 0.02564)
$950$505.26% (50 / 950 = 0.05263)
$925$758.11% (75 / 925 = 0.08108)

Part 2: a lower price means a higher yield, because the payoff at maturity is fixed. Part 3: any layered rate with a benchmark plus add-ons whose total adds up and is labeled as made up (the lesson's example is 4.0 + 0.5 + 1.0 = 5.5 percent).

8.02 - From a Vote to a Payment (completion)

Part 1 key ($162,000, 30 years). The extra over the loan is the monthly increase times 360, which equals the change in total interest because principal and term are the same.

StepMonthly increaseTimes 360
2.875% to 3.875% ($672.13 to $761.78)$89.65$32,274.00
3.875% to 4.875% ($761.78 to $857.32)$95.54$34,394.40
4.875% to 5.875% ($857.32 to $958.29)$100.97$36,349.20

Part 2: the FOMC raises its target range; banks pay more for short-term money and earn more on reserves; banks raise loan rates; borrowing costs more; spending cools and price increases ease. The Fed's choice is hard because of its two goals (maximum employment and stable prices). A fixed-rate loan already signed does not change; a new borrower or a variable-rate borrower is affected.

8.03 - Build the Schedule (Excel; rubric, 5 criteria x 2 points)

Reference values for $162,000, 3.875 percent, 30 years (lesson-8-03-teacher-key-amortization-schedule.xlsx):

  • Payment $761.78 (exact value $761.784); matches the Loan Estimate.
  • Payment 1: interest $523.13, principal $238.65, balance $161,761.35.
  • Payment 60: balance $146,227.42 with rounded cents (a student who does not round the payment will see $146,227.14; accept within a dollar).
  • Tipping point: payment 147 (146: interest $380.90, principal $380.88; 147: interest $379.67, principal $382.11), balance $117,192.03.
  • Total interest: $112,240.80 (360 x $761.78 minus $162,000) or $112,243.70 (sum of the schedule's rounded interest, when the last payment clears the remaining balance). The few-dollar gap is the answer to the "why" sentence: payments are rounded to the cent, so a small balance remains after payment 360 and the last payment is slightly larger.
  • Lever options: 15-year term $1,188.17 and $51,870.60 total interest (down $60,370.20); 20 percent down $677.14 and $99,770.40 (down $12,470.40); $100 added to every payment pays off in 290 months and saves about $24,576 (needs an extra-payment column).
  • After five years about 90.3 percent of the loan is still owed.

Grading shortcut: check the Inputs sheet values and the tipping point first, then open one row of the schedule to confirm it contains formulas. The chart needs axis labels and a title.

8.04 - A Plan Before the Promise (rubric, 5 criteria x 2 points)

Each student invents a purchase, so check method, not numbers. The seven steps: purpose, price and down payment, rate, term, total cost of credit, budget, risks. A model answer to compare against is the lesson's car example: $20,000 at 6 percent, 48 months $469.70 a month and $2,545.60 interest; 60 months $386.66 and $3,199.60; the longer loan costs $654.00 more and keeps the student in debt another year. The total-cost-of-credit rule: count interest plus required fees and insurance, and leave out property taxes and homeowner's insurance (the lesson's sample comes to about $124,801). The closing sentence answers "What am I paying for the privilege of borrowing?"

Module 8 Project - The Borrower's Brief (50 points; rubric 5 x 10)

All offers are fictional; each is $162,000 over 30 years, fixed rate.

OfferRateClosing costsMonthly P&ITotal interest (payments x 360 minus loan)
A3.875%$8,054$761.78$112,240.80
B3.625%$11,000$738.80$103,968.00
C4.125%$6,000$785.13$120,646.80

Cost of borrowing during the stay (interest paid up to that month, from a rounded-cent schedule, plus closing costs). Accept differences of a few dollars:

BuyerStayABCLowest
14 years$32,250.08$33,599.34$31,796.42C
27 years$49,056.54$49,250.08$49,766.37A (B is only $193.54 more)
315 years$87,040.00$84,448.76$90,574.25B

Break-even for B against A: extra closing costs $2,946 divided by the monthly saving $22.98 is about 128 months (10.7 years) if you count only the payment difference. If you count interest paid plus closing costs (which also credits B's faster principal paydown), B overtakes A in month 91 (about 7.6 years). Either approach is acceptable if the student states which one is used. Crossovers on the interest-plus-closing-costs basis: A beats C from month 62; B beats C from month 76.

A strong memo ties the recommendation to the buyer's stay, explains that a lower rate is not automatically cheaper once fees are counted, explains that Treasury yields are the benchmark that lenders build on and that Fed decisions move short-term rates and expectations, notes that a fixed rate protects against future rate rises but not against income loss, moving early, or fees, and ends with the "privilege of borrowing" sentence.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Every decision you make is really an economics problem in disguise: something given up so something else can be gained. This assignment asks you to take one real decision from your own life and examine it the way an economist would.

Reading and Analyzing the Production Possibilities Curve
Assignment · 20 pts
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Lesson 1.02 introduced the Production Possibilities Curve (PPC) as one line of vocabulary. This assignment asks you to actually read one — to look at a real PPC diagram and use it to reason about efficiency, scarcity, and opportunity cost the way an economist would, rather than just defining the term.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What does the shape and position of a production possibilities curve reveal about scarcity, efficiency, and opportunity cost?
📈 THE DIAGRAM
This economy produces only two kinds of goods: Consumer Goods and Capital Goods. The curve shows every combination the economy can produce at full, efficient use of its current resources and technology.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS

1. Look at points A, B, C, and D on the diagram above. For each point, state whether it represents efficient, inefficient, or unattainable production, and explain how you can tell from where it sits relative to the curve.

2. Compare points A and B. If the economy moved from point A to point B, what would it be giving up, and what would it be gaining? Write this as a specific opportunity cost statement (e.g., "moving from A to B costs ___ in order to gain ___").

3. Point C sits inside the curve. Name one real reason an economy might actually be producing at a point like C instead of on the curve (think about unemployment, unused factories, or underused resources).

4. Point D sits outside the curve — currently unattainable. Name two things that could cause the entire curve to shift outward, making a point like D possible in the future.

5. In 3–5 sentences, explain how this one diagram manages to show scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost all at once.

Supplementary · Lesson 2.03
How Are Workers' Earnings Determined?
Assignment · 20 pts
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Lesson 2.03 covered price and competition in markets for goods. Labor is bought and sold in a market too — the "good" being traded is a worker's time and skill, the "price" is the wage. This assignment applies the same supply-and-demand logic you already know to the specific question of why some jobs pay more than others.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Why does the labor market pay some workers far more than others, and what would make that gap change?
📈 THE LABOR MARKET
Like any market, a labor market has a supply curve (workers willing to work at each wage) and a demand curve (employers willing to hire at each wage). Where they cross sets the equilibrium wage and the number of workers employed.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS

1. Using the graph above, explain in your own words what sets the equilibrium wage (point E) for a given job — what does the supply curve represent, and what does the demand curve represent, in a labor market specifically?

2. Choose two real occupations with a clear pay difference (for example: a surgeon and a retail cashier, or a software engineer and a fast-food worker — pick your own pair). Explain the wage gap using both: (a) differences in labor supply — how much training, education, or licensing is required to do the job, which limits how many people can supply that labor; and (b) differences in labor demand — how much value each worker's output is worth to an employer (this is called their productivity, or marginal revenue product).

3. Pick one of your two occupations. Predict and explain, using supply-and-demand shift language ("the supply curve shifts right/left," "the demand curve shifts right/left"), what would happen to its equilibrium wage and the number of people employed in it if: (a) demand for that skill suddenly rose (for example, because of new technology that needs it), and (b) the supply of qualified workers suddenly rose (for example, because a new training program produced a wave of new graduates).

4. Name one real factor that can keep a wage from settling at its market equilibrium (for example: minimum wage laws, labor unions, or occupational licensing requirements) and briefly explain how it affects employment in that market.

Module 6 Project
The Fork in the Road
Culminating Assessment · 50 pts
🧭 THE TASK
The Depression was not scheduled in advance. It grew out of decisions that real people made with the information they had. Choose one decision point from Module 6, and write a brief that studies it the way a careful economist and historian would: what was chosen, what the evidence shows, what the other road might have been, and where the evidence runs out.
✅ CHOOSE ONE DECISION POINT
  • The Fed's 1929 argument over raising the discount rate versus pressuring banks directly
  • The Fed's raising of its discount rate in October 1931, after Britain left the gold standard
  • The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act (1930)
  • The Revenue Act of 1932
  • The bank holiday and the Emergency Banking Act (1933)
  • The NIRA or the AAA (1933)
  • The Fed's doubling of reserve requirements in 1936 and 1937
📝 WHAT YOUR BRIEF MUST CONTAIN
Part 1. The Choice (about 300 words)
What was decided, who decided it, and what did they know at the time? Do not judge with hindsight. Show that other choices were available.
Part 2. The Evidence (about 400 words)
Use at least four sources: at least two from this course (your lessons, including a primary-source passage from Lesson 6.04 or 6.05 where it fits) and at least two outside sources you have read yourself, such as Federal Reserve History, the FDIC, the National Archives, the Library of Congress, or the National Bureau of Economic Research. Cite each one with footnotes or a works cited list. Quote only words you have actually read. If two sources disagree, report both.
Part 3. The Other Road (about 300 words)
Describe one plausible alternative choice. Using the tools of the course, explain what would likely have followed, and answer the question compared with what? Say who would have borne the costs of your alternative, and who would have gained.
Part 4. The Verdict (about 200 words)
Judge the decision by the first-order economic problem. Describe the decision-makers by stable traits, not by a single act. Say where the evidence runs out, and end with the strongest objection to your own argument.
Format. Word document, about 1,200 to 1,500 words. You may submit a recorded presentation of 8 to 10 minutes instead of a document. It is graded by the same rubric, and every part above is still required.
📁 M365 REMINDER

🧭 THE TASK
A first-time home buyer must choose among three loan offers for the same house. Your job is to write the buyer a memo that picks one, shows the numbers, and explains the risks in plain words. All three offers are fictional, made up for this project.
📋 THE THREE OFFERS (FICTIONAL)
OfferLenderLoanRate (fixed)Closing costs
AHarbor Federal (fictional)$162,000, 30 years3.875%$8,054
BLakeshore Credit Union (fictional)$162,000, 30 years3.625%$11,000
CSummit Mortgage (fictional)$162,000, 30 years4.125%$6,000
Offer B's higher closing costs include a fee paid to buy the lower rate. Assume the buyer pays the closing costs in cash, and that mortgage insurance, escrow, and any prepayment penalty are the same for all three offers, so you can leave them out of your comparison.
🏠 THE THREE BUYERS (FICTIONAL)
BuyerPlan
Buyer 1Expects to move for work in about 4 years
Buyer 2Expects to stay in the house for about 7 years
Buyer 3Expects to stay in the house for about 15 years
Choose one buyer for Parts 2 through 5.
📝 WHAT YOUR MEMO MUST CONTAIN
Part 1. The Numbers
For each offer, find the monthly principal and interest payment, and the total interest over 30 years (360 times the payment, minus $162,000). You can reuse the workbook you built in Lesson 8.03: copy the sheets, and change the rate.
Part 2. The Buyer's Stay
Choose one of the three buyers above. For each offer, find the cost of borrowing during the buyer's stay: the interest paid up to that time, plus the closing costs. (Your Lesson 8.03 schedule shows the interest column. Add it up to the right month.) Show the results in a table, and say which offer costs least for that buyer.
Part 3. Break-Even
Offer B costs more at closing and less each month than Offer A. Find the number of months it takes for B's lower payment to make up its higher closing costs, and explain what that number means for the buyer you chose.
Part 4. Plain-Language Explanation
In about 200 words, explain to the buyer how the Treasury benchmark and the Federal Reserve's decisions are part of the rate the buyer is offered, and what a fixed rate does and does not protect against.
Part 5. Recommendation and Risks
State your recommendation in one sentence. Name two risks the buyer still carries (think of income, moving earlier than planned, or fees) and what the buyer could do about each. Close with the sentence the lesson asks every borrower to answer: What am I paying for the privilege of borrowing?
Format. Word memo of about 800 to 1,200 words, plus a table (an Excel appendix is optional). The memo is the deliverable. You may attach an Excel appendix to show your work.

questions.text: How does a deficit differ from the national debt?

answers.text: A deficit is one year's shortfall of revenue, while the national debt is the running total of past deficits not yet repaid
The debt is one year's shortfall, and the deficit is the running total

questions.feedback_general: A surplus happens when revenue exceeds spending, as in the late 1990s.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say the debt-to-GDP ratio matters more than the raw debt figure?

answers.text: It compares the debt with the size of the economy, so $20 trillion against a larger economy is easier to carry
GDP is the same in every country

questions.feedback_general: After World War II the ratio exceeded 100 percent, but rapid growth brought it down without a crisis.

questions.text: Technically, a recession is:

answers.text: Two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth

questions.feedback_general: The Great Depression and the 2007-2009 Great Recession are the starkest U.S. examples.

questions.text: Why does inflation favor debtors over lenders?

answers.text: A fixed-rate loan is repaid in dollars that buy less, so the borrower repays less in real terms than was borrowed

questions.feedback_general: The lender loses purchasing power on what is repaid.

questions.text: Why did Fed Chairman Paul Volcker raise interest rates above 15 percent in the early 1980s?

answers.text: To break double-digit inflation, a policy that caused a sharp recession but restored long-term price stability

questions.feedback_general: Hyperinflation is far more severe. The Fed generally targets about 2 percent as healthy.

questions.text: A government sets a price ceiling below the market's equilibrium price. What does the lesson say usually results?

answers.text: A shortage, such as the long gasoline lines of the 1970s

questions.feedback_general: Rationing by inconvenience appears once the price signal stops doing its normal job.

questions.text: A factory dumps waste into a river, and downstream residents bear the costs. This is:

answers.text: A negative externality, since the costs fall on people outside the transaction and never show up in the factory's prices

questions.feedback_general: A Pigovian tax is one response, because it makes the polluter pay something closer to the true social cost.

questions.text: A buyer purchases $1,000 of stock with $100 of her own money and $900 borrowed. The stock price then falls 10 percent. What is the result?

answers.text: Her $100 is gone, and the stock is worth exactly what she owes
She owes only $800 because the loan shrinks with the price

questions.feedback_general: The stock is now worth $900. The loan is still $900. Borrowing multiplied the gains on the way up and the losses on the way down by the same amount.

questions.text: A farmer owes the bank $1,000, and in a normal year her grain sells for $1,000. Prices then fall by a quarter, so the same crop sells for $750. About how much more grain does she now need to sell to pay the same $1,000 debt?
questions.feedback_general: $1,000 divided by $750 is about 1.33. The debt did not shrink, but the price did, so the debt grew heavier in real terms.

questions.text: The lesson treats the 1920s boom as a fake, because production and jobs were actually low.
questions.feedback_general: The boom was real. Factories turned out more than ever, and unemployment in 1929 was only about 3 percent. The lesson asks what held the boom up, not whether it existed.

questions.text: In 1929 the New York Fed wanted to slow stock speculation by raising which interest rate?

answers.text: The discount rate, the rate the Fed charges banks that borrow from it
The rate on installment loans for cars

questions.feedback_general: The Federal Reserve Board preferred pressuring member banks directly. The New York Fed wanted a higher discount rate. Both sides had a point.

questions.text: A classmate says, "The crash was certain the moment stock prices began to rise." Which reply best fits the lesson's idea of contingency?

answers.text: Real people faced real choices in the 1920s, and different choices would have led to a different outcome
She is right, because every boom ends in a crash
She is right, because farmers caused the whole Depression
She is wrong, because the Fed had no choices at all

questions.feedback_general: Contingency means the past was open when it was the present. Lenders could have required more than 10 percent down, and the Fed leaders could have chosen differently.

questions.text: Why is a stock market crash not automatically a depression?

answers.text: A crash always ends within a week
It destroys paper wealth, but a depression also requires the economy to lose its ability to lend, pay, and move money
A crash only affects the banking system in other countries

questions.feedback_general: Stocks had fallen sharply before without a decade of misery. The banking collapse that followed is what turned a bad year into a catastrophe.

questions.text: A bank holds $100 in deposits, keeps $10 in cash, and has lent $90. If 20 percent of depositors ask for their money on the same day, how much more cash does the bank need than it has?
questions.feedback_general: Twenty percent of $100 is $20. The bank has $10. It cannot collect its loans overnight, so it closes even if many of its loans are sound.

questions.text: In 1930, a family whose bank failed was protected by federal deposit insurance.
questions.feedback_general: Deposit insurance did not exist in 1930. A family that lost its bank lost its savings, which is why a rumor could start a run.

questions.text: After Great Britain left the gold standard on September 21, 1931, why did the New York Fed raise its discount rate in early October?

answers.text: Foreigners were swapping dollars for gold, and gold was flowing out of the United States

questions.feedback_general: The textbook way to attract gold is to raise rates. But higher rates made borrowing harder for banks in the middle of a banking crisis. The Fed faced a real dilemma.

questions.text: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued that the Depression became so severe mainly because:

answers.text: Congress raised the top income tax rate
The Fed let the money supply collapse, turning an ordinary recession into a depression
The stock market never recovered its 1929 high
Banks lent too little to farmers in the 1920s

questions.feedback_general: The Fed's history reports the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent from fall 1930 to winter 1933. Another view stresses collapsing spending and confidence, and many economists combine the two.

questions.text: Economists date the peak of the business cycle at August 1929 and the trough at March 1933. About how long did the contraction last?
questions.feedback_general: August 1929 to March 1933 is 43 months. A normal recession lasts months, not more than three and a half years.

questions.text: Stanley Lebergott puts 1933 unemployment near 24.9 percent, and Michael Darby near 20.6 percent. Why do two careful economists differ?

answers.text: One of them made an arithmetic mistake
Lebergott counted people on government work projects as unemployed, and Darby counted them as employed
The government sent each of them different data

questions.feedback_general: They answer slightly different questions. Either number tells the same story: a huge share of workers had no regular job.

questions.text: A worker who kept a steady paycheck during the early 1930s could be better off, because falling prices stretched the same wages further.
questions.feedback_general: The Depression did not hit everyone equally. Debt, savings, and type of work made a big difference, and the people hurt most had the least cushion.

questions.text: What was the political origin of the name "Hooverville"?

answers.text: It was a partisan label, first printed in 1930 by a Democratic Party publicity director, after President Hoover
Residents voted to name the camps after Hoover
It was an official federal term for relief housing

questions.feedback_general: According to HistoryLink, Charles Michelson used it in a New York Times article about a Chicago camp. It was a political label from the start.

questions.text: How did the Federal Emergency Relief Administration (May 1933) differ from relief help under Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation?

answers.text: It gave grants to states and cities instead of loans
It paid unemployed workers directly in gold

questions.feedback_general: A loan has to be repaid, and states with falling incomes did not want more debt. Grants removed that obstacle.

questions.text: What did the Soil Conservation Act of April 27, 1935 create?

answers.text: The Soil Conservation Service, a permanent agency in the Department of Agriculture, with Hugh Hammond Bennett as its first chief
A program that paid farmers to plow more land

questions.feedback_general: Congress acted within weeks of the dust storm that reached Washington. The agency exists today as the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

questions.text: Which sequence best describes how the Dust Bowl developed?

answers.text: Drought came first, which caused falling wheat prices, which caused farmers to plow
Falling prices and fixed debts led farmers to plow more, the grass was lost, drought came, and the wind lifted the topsoil
The Soil Conservation Service plowed the grass, and drought followed
Banks demanded that farmers stop plowing, which caused the storms

questions.feedback_general: No step needed a villain. Weather, farming practices, and debt together produced the disaster, and removing any one of them changes the story.

questions.text: A farm normally sells $1,000 of wheat. Of that, $400 pays the loan, $300 pays for seed and fuel, and $300 supports the family. In a drought year the farm sells only $500. The costs stay the same. How large is the shortfall?
questions.feedback_general: The farm needs $1,000 and has $500. The loan payment alone ($400) takes most of the year's income, so the farmer must borrow more, sell equipment, or give up land.

questions.text: Why does a tenant farmer face a different kind of risk than a farmer with a mortgage?

answers.text: A tenant has no ownership of the land to protect and can lose the right to farm when the owner ends the arrangement
A tenant owns the land but rents the crops
A tenant has no risk when crops fail
A tenant can never be removed from the land

questions.feedback_general: A tenant has no mortgage to lose, but also no ownership. Owners, tenants, and hired hands faced the same drought with very different protection.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call blowing dust an externality?

answers.text: The dust only harmed the farmer who left a field bare
Dust from a stripped field settled on neighbors who never agreed to bear that cost
The dust raised wheat prices for everyone

questions.feedback_general: Protecting soil works best when many farmers do it together, which is hard to arrange without a shared rule or shared support. That is why conservation became a government matter.

questions.text: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act (June 1930) is mainly an example of which policy lever?
questions.feedback_general: It raised duties on more than 20,000 imported goods. Other countries answered with tariffs of their own, and historians generally see the act as having made the Depression worse.

questions.text: Why did many economists criticize the 1932 Revenue Act, which raised the top income tax rate from 25 to 63 percent?

answers.text: Raising taxes in a contraction reduces spending power when spending is already falling

questions.feedback_general: The usual advice in a recession is to cut taxes or raise spending. Hoover feared deficits would scare lenders, and he was following the textbook of his day.

questions.text: Which list puts the 1933 bank rescue steps in the correct order?

answers.text: Emergency Banking Act, bank holiday, banks begin reopening
Banks begin reopening, bank holiday, Emergency Banking Act
Bank holiday declared (March 6), Emergency Banking Act (March 9), banks begin reopening (March 13 to 15)
FDIC begins insuring deposits, bank holiday, Emergency Banking Act

questions.feedback_general: The holiday stopped the runs and gave examiners time to sort sound banks from broken ones. The FDIC began insuring deposits later, on January 1, 1934.

questions.text: Deposit insurance removes the cause of a bank run, but it can also create moral hazard, because protected depositors have less reason to check how risky their bank is.
questions.feedback_general: People shielded from the cost of a risk may take more of it. That is why deposit insurance comes with rules and inspections.

questions.text: What was the National Industrial Recovery Act (June 1933) trying to stop?

answers.text: The spiral of falling wages and prices, by setting wage and price floors under industries

questions.feedback_general: Industry codes set minimum wages and maximum hours and discouraged cutthroat price cutting. Critics said such codes can protect large firms and keep businesses from hiring.

questions.text: The Social Security Act of 1935 did not cover which workers?

answers.text: Agricultural laborers and domestic servants in private homes

questions.feedback_general: In 1935 a large share of the workforce, including a majority of Black workers, worked on farms or in other people's homes.

questions.text: The SSA historian Larry DeWitt points to administrative feasibility, while other scholars stress that the exclusion fell on most Black workers. How can both readings be accepted at once?

answers.text: Both say racial bias was the only cause
One concerns why Congress acted, and the other concerns what happened as a result
Both are about the AAA, not Social Security

questions.feedback_general: A careful student can accept that the law was shaped by practical limits and also that its effect fell heavily on those workers.

questions.text: In United States v. Butler (January 6, 1936), the Supreme Court:

answers.text: Struck down the tax that paid for the AAA's subsidies

questions.feedback_general: The Court's ruling in Schechter (May 27, 1935) had already held part of the NIRA unconstitutional. Neither program continued in its original form.

questions.text: The business cycle dates show the economy turned down again in 1937. Which describes that contraction?

answers.text: It ran from May 1937 to June 1938, 13 months, after a 50-month expansion
It was caused only by the FDIC

questions.feedback_general: The cause of the 1937 recession is still debated. One argument points to the Fed doubling reserve requirements, while other economists found the effect may have been small.

questions.text: Christina Romer argued that nearly all of the recovery before 1942 came from what?

answers.text: Monetary expansion, as gold flowing into the United States swelled the money supply

questions.feedback_general: On her chain, money lowers real interest rates, which encourages investment and durable-goods spending. This is one economist's analysis, and critics argue fiscal effects may be understated.

quizzes.title: Lesson 6.04 - Primary Source Exercise
quizzes.description:
"The writer, after 24 years spent in studying the soils of the United States, is of the opinion that soil erosion is the biggest problem confronting the farmers of the Nation over a tremendous part of its agricultural lands. It seems scarcely necessary to state the perfectly obvious fact that a very large part of this impoverishment and wastage has taken place since the clearing of the forests, the breaking of the prairie sod, and the overgrazing of pasture lands."

H. H. Bennett and W. R. Chapline, Soil Erosion: A National Menace, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Circular No. 33, April 1928.

questions.text: On what does Bennett base his opinion that soil erosion is the biggest problem facing farmers?

answers.text: Twenty-four years spent studying the soils of the United States

questions.feedback_general: He cites a long record of experience, not a single event. He states a conclusion without panic.

questions.text: Which statement does the passage best support about the cause of the damage?

answers.text: Much of the damage followed human land use: clearing forests, breaking prairie sod, and overgrazing
The damage was caused by Eastern factories

questions.feedback_general: Bennett says the impoverishment has "taken place since" the clearing, the sod-breaking, and the overgrazing. He argues human choices created the vulnerability.

questions.text: A Plains farmer reads this circular in 1928 and agrees with it. According to the lesson, which obstacle would most likely still keep that farmer plowing?

answers.text: The circular was written for city readers
A mortgage payment was due, and plowing more land was the way to earn it
The farmer owned too little land to plow

questions.feedback_general: The person who sees the danger may still be unable to afford the safe choice. That is the economic trap the lesson describes.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what does Bennett's passage leave out?

answers.text: How a farmer should pay for new practices

questions.feedback_general: That gap is where economics enters the story. Good advice about soil does not tell a heavily indebted farmer how to afford the change.

quizzes.title: Lesson 6.05 - Primary Source Exercise
quizzes.description:
"So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself--nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance."

"Our greatest primary task is to put people to work."

Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1933 (public domain; text from the Avalon Project, Yale Law School).

questions.text: In the first passage, what does Roosevelt say paralyzes "needed efforts to convert retreat into advance"?
questions.feedback_general: He names fear itself as the enemy, not a person and not a policy.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say this sentence is an economic claim and not only a speech?

answers.text: In a bank run, fear is the cause; if people stop believing banks are safe, banks fail no matter how sound they are
Fear always raises the price of gold
Fear is the only thing that affects stock prices
Roosevelt promised to end all bank failures that day

questions.feedback_general: Nothing about the banks' assets changed in a few days in March 1933. What changed was what people believed about them.

questions.text: Suppose federal deposit insurance had existed in 1930. Based on the lesson, what would most likely have happened to the runs that began that November?

answers.text: They would have had no effect on the Fed
The gold standard would have ended sooner
Depositors would have had little reason to rush, removing a main cause of the runs

questions.feedback_general: If your deposit is guaranteed, you have no reason to rush to the bank. The rule works because it makes a certain kind of panic unnecessary.

questions.text: Why does the sentence "Our greatest primary task is to put people to work" fit the lesson's discussion of relief?

answers.text: It shows Roosevelt opposed all government help
Many officials came to prefer work relief, because it keeps a worker's skills and dignity and leaves something behind, such as a road or a school
It shows relief should only come from charities
It shows Roosevelt wanted to cut the federal budget

questions.feedback_general: A job is more than income. It is a place in the community.

questions.text: Which statement best explains why borrowing made the 1920s boom fragile?

answers.text: Borrowers owe fixed payments no matter what happens to their income, so a drop in income is hard to absorb

questions.feedback_general: Installment credit and margin buying were tools, but each future payment comes out of future income. If that income stops, the payments do not.

questions.text: A buyer purchases $2,000 of stock with $200 down and borrows $1,800. At what price is the stock worth only what she owes?
questions.feedback_general: Once the stock is worth $1,800, her stake is gone. A 10 percent fall erased a 10 percent down payment.

questions.text: A lender demands more money immediately from a margin buyer whose stock fell below the loan. This demand is called:
