questions.feedback_general: If the buyer could not pay, the lender sold the stock. Millions of small forced sales could push prices down further.

questions.text: Wheat prices fell, so Plains farmers plowed more land. Why can each decision be sensible while the result is harmful?

answers.text: Each farmer responded to the price signal, but nobody was adding up what a thousand farmers doing it at once meant

questions.feedback_general: The signal said "plow more" to every farmer. The result was too much wheat for the market and soil with nothing to hold it.

questions.text: In what way does the Dow's fall (381.17 on September 3, 1929 to 41.22 on July 8, 1932) illustrate why a crash is not the whole story of the Depression?

answers.text: Economists date the peak of the economy in August 1929, and the worst came later, when banks failed and the money supply shrank
It shows the Dow measures bank failures

questions.feedback_general: The economy was already turning down before October 1929, and the banking collapse was what turned a downturn into a depression.

questions.text: A bank with $10 in cash and $90 in loans faces a run. Why might it close even if most of its loans are sound?

answers.text: Depositors are always wrong to ask for their money
Borrowers cannot repay overnight, and if every bank sells loans at once, buyers offer very little
The Fed forbids banks from keeping cash

questions.feedback_general: A bank can be sound and still run out of cash at the moment people demand it. The harm then spreads to businesses that counted on its loans.

questions.text: According to the FDIC, about how many banks suspended operations from 1930 to 1933?
questions.feedback_general: There were fewer than 25,000 banks in the country, so this was a very large share of them.

questions.text: The Fed's history calls its most serious failure its "failure to stem the decline in the supply of money." Which fact supports that judgment?

answers.text: The money supply fell by nearly 30 percent from fall 1930 to winter 1933

questions.feedback_general: Prices fell by about the same proportion. Other measures show a drop of roughly a quarter to a third.

questions.text: Falling prices make debts heavier. Which statement explains why?

answers.text: Lenders raise the interest rate when prices fall
A fixed number of dollars owed is harder to earn when the dollars you earn buy and bring in less
Debts are always forgiven when prices fall

questions.feedback_general: This is the same logic as the farmer who owed $1,000 when her crop price fell by a quarter.

questions.text: Why do economists fear a steady fall in prices more than a small rise?

answers.text: When prices are falling, people wait to buy, and if everyone waits, sales fall further

questions.feedback_general: Add the fixed debts, and you can see why the spiral of lost jobs, falling prices, and cost cutting was so hard to stop.

questions.text: The peak of the business cycle was August 1929, and the trough was March 1933. The trough marks:

answers.text: The lowest point, with the banking system in collapse

questions.feedback_general: The expansion that followed ran 50 months, to a new peak in May 1937.

questions.text: A town has 4,000 workers, and 25 percent are unemployed. How many are out of work?
questions.feedback_general: One worker in four is 1,000 of 4,000. Their lost spending then reduces other people's income.

questions.text: Before the 1930s, most help for jobless Americans came from which sources?
questions.feedback_general: This was often enough for ordinary downturns. In a depression, local charities ran out of money just as more families needed help.

questions.text: Hugh Hammond Bennett and W. R. Chapline wrote Soil Erosion: A National Menace in what year, and what did it show?

answers.text: 1928, seven years before Black Sunday, which showed the problem had already been named
1931, at the start of the drought

questions.feedback_general: The 1928 circular blamed clearing, sod-breaking, and overgrazing. The Dust Bowl drought began in 1931.

questions.text: A foreclosure occurs when:

answers.text: A lender takes and sells property because the borrower cannot pay the loan

questions.feedback_general: For a farm family, the farm is a home, a job, and a way of life, so losing it means losing all of them at once.

questions.text: The founders saw secure property as a pillar of freedom because:

answers.text: A person who owns something can say no to a boss, a landlord, or a ruler
Property rights are only about the law

questions.feedback_general: The Dust Bowl shows another side: a farm that blows away is a farm no deed can protect.

questions.text: Which describes the 1932 Revenue Act as the lesson presents it?

answers.text: It cut the top income tax rate to 25 percent
It raised the top rate from 25 percent to 63 percent and broadened who paid

questions.feedback_general: Critics said it made the downturn worse. Supporters of Hoover said he feared large deficits would scare lenders.

questions.text: The Reconstruction Finance Corporation, created in January 1932, was mainly:

answers.text: A government lender to banks, railroads, and other institutions in trouble

questions.feedback_general: It was Hoover's most direct federal intervention. Critics said it came late and was too small.

questions.text: The Emergency Banking Act of March 9, 1933 gave the government power to:
questions.feedback_general: Banks reopened in stages from March 13 to March 15, and the public put about two-thirds of the withdrawn currency back into banks by the end of the month.

questions.text: Which pairing of tool and example is correct?

answers.text: Monetary policy: the Fed buying government securities to add money to the banking system

questions.feedback_general: Trade policy changes the rules for goods crossing a border, fiscal policy changes taxes and spending, monetary policy changes money and borrowing costs, and regulation changes the rules for businesses and banks.

questions.text: The AAA tried to raise farm prices by paying farmers to grow less. What economic idea was it applying?

answers.text: If supply falls, price tends to rise

questions.feedback_general: Supporters said higher crop prices would make debts easier to pay. Critics asked whether it was wise to pay farmers to produce less when people were hungry, and who ends up paying.

questions.text: The AAA's subsidies were paid for by a tax on processors, such as cotton mill owners. The lesson says who ultimately pays the tax:

answers.text: Is always the person who writes the check
Is decided by how buyers and sellers respond, since the processor can try to pass it on in higher prices or lower payments to farmers

questions.feedback_general: Economists call this the question of incidence. It applies to taxes and tariffs as well as pensions.

questions.text: Which statement about the end of the Depression is most accurate?

answers.text: Economists agree that war spending alone ended it
Economists weigh money, government spending, and war mobilization differently, and the weights remain in dispute

questions.feedback_general: You can be confident of what is documented and honest about what is not. A claim that the New Deal "worked" or "failed" needs a comparison: compared with what?

questions.text: Who was left out of the Social Security Act of 1935, and what did the lesson ask you to keep in mind?

answers.text: Agricultural laborers and domestic servants were left out, and where a program draws its line changes who benefits and who must find another way

questions.feedback_general: This is the idea of incidence applied to coverage. Whatever the motive, the effect fell heavily on a large share of Black workers.

questions.text: In judging the New Deal against the first-order economic problem, the lesson's fair summary is that:

answers.text: The bank rescue and the FDIC worked quickly and have lasted, some ambitious programs were struck down or reshaped, and the economy did not fully recover in the 1930s

questions.feedback_general: The summary reports what happened without choosing a verdict. That is what honesty in scholarship looks like.

questions.text: In the Manifesto, how are the bourgeoisie and the proletariat sorted from each other?

answers.text: By how much money each person earns
By whether they live in a city or a village
By whether they own capital or live by selling their labor
By which country they were born in

questions.feedback_general: The theory sorts people by their relationship to capital: the tools, buildings, and land used to make goods.

questions.text: Marx and Engels wrote with no admiration at all for what the bourgeoisie had built.
questions.feedback_general: They admired its productive power: it had "established the world market" and built cities, ships, railroads, and factories. Their complaint was that workers did not share in the results.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what is the narrower target of the Manifesto's phrase "Abolition of private property"?

answers.text: The ownership of capital: the factories, land, and other productive assets that let one class hire another

questions.feedback_general: If you stop reading at the sentence, it sounds as if the authors want your phone and your savings. Read further, and the target is the ownership of capital.

questions.text: Which of Marx and Engels's ten measures has a close relative in the United States today?
questions.feedback_general: The United States also has a progressive income tax and free public schools. What set the Manifesto apart was the combination and the goal of moving almost all productive property into the hands of the state.

questions.text: Marx and Engels expected revolution to come first in the most industrial countries. What actually happened?

answers.text: The first communist revolutions came in Russia and China, which were mostly farming countries at the time
Revolutions came only in the United States

questions.feedback_general: A failed prediction does not erase a theory, but it deserves to be noticed and tested against what actually happened.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say the provisional government's choice to stay in World War I mattered?

answers.text: Soldiers and city workers wanted peace and bread, and the weak government could provide neither

questions.feedback_general: Into that gap stepped the Bolsheviks, a small, disciplined party led by Lenin. None of it was certain, and a different choice could have changed the story.

questions.text: Which list names the three main parts of War Communism?

answers.text: A grain tax, private trade, and foreign investment
Grain requisition, nationalization of industry, and a ban on private trade

questions.feedback_general: The policy fit the Manifesto's goals: the state took ownership of the means of production and put planning in the place of markets.

questions.text: The grain harvest fell from 80.1 million tons in 1913 to 46.5 million tons in 1920. About what percent was that drop?
questions.feedback_general: 80.1 minus 46.5 is 33.6 million tons, and 33.6 divided by 80.1 is about 0.42. The war and civil war also wrecked fields and railroads, so the policy was not the only cause.

questions.text: What did the New Economic Policy change for farmers in 1921?

answers.text: It required farmers to give all their grain to the state
It replaced seizure with a fixed tax in grain and let farmers sell the rest
It placed all farms under army control

questions.feedback_general: The state kept the largest industries and the banks, but the bargain with the farmer changed. Farm output began to recover.

questions.text: In 1921 Lenin called War Communism "too hasty, rigid, unprepared 'communism'" and also said it was "necessitated by the war." What does the lesson suggest about reading this?

answers.text: It proves the policy was a success
Willingness to look at results is a useful quality, while blaming the war for everything is an excuse historians should test, not accept
It shows the NEP was never needed

questions.feedback_general: Both parts of the quotation matter. The lesson asks you to hold the admission and the excuse together.

questions.text: What was Gosplan?

answers.text: The Soviet state planning commission that drew up targets for the whole economy

questions.feedback_general: Its targets became the basis of the first Five-Year Plan, which began in 1928.

questions.text: How does a command economy answer the question "What to produce?"

answers.text: Buyers' demand, shown by prices and profits

questions.feedback_general: Under the Five-Year Plan the answer was heavy industry: steel, coal, electric power, and machines.

questions.text: A boot factory is told to produce 10,000 pairs and is judged only on that count. Which result does the lesson's example predict?

answers.text: The factory makes one size and style from the cheapest leather, meets the count, and stores get boots few people can use

questions.feedback_general: The plan counted pairs. It did not count whether anyone could use them. A planner would need information about sizes and tastes from the whole country.

questions.text: In the lesson's figures, Ukraine's harvest in 1931 was 18.3 million tons and the demand was 7.7 million tons. About what percent of the harvest was demanded?
questions.feedback_general: 7.7 divided by 18.3 is about 0.42. A demand that large leaves little margin for the farm family's food, seed, and animal feed. The lesson notes these figures come from a standard reference article and are approximate.

questions.text: Which statement fairly describes the historians' debate about the famine of 1932 to 1933?

answers.text: All historians agree it was a deliberate plan to kill
All historians agree weather alone caused it
Scholars disagree about intent, but all agree an economic plan enforced without regard to farmers was followed by millions of deaths

questions.feedback_general: Getty, Davies, and Wheatcroft stress "bungling and rigidity." Ellman argues that knowingly keeping policies that cause mass death can be a form of intent. The lesson gives estimates of about 3 million to nearly 9 million dead.

questions.text: What is the knowledge problem?

answers.text: The knowledge needed to run an economy is scattered among millions of people and cannot all be gathered in one place
A shortage of paper for government reports
The fact that planners never studied mathematics

questions.feedback_general: A shop owner, a farmer, and a truck driver each know something no official report holds.

questions.text: In the tin example, what does a buyer need to know in order to respond sensibly to a shortage?
questions.feedback_general: A price is a message that carries information without telling people why. The shortage is eased without anyone giving an order.

questions.text: Under the Five-Year Plan, what was a manager's best strategy?

answers.text: To please buyers as much as possible
To make the plan easy to meet: ask for generous supplies, promise less than you can do, and avoid risks

questions.feedback_general: A manager's reward came from meeting the plan, not from serving buyers. Targets were often raised after being met, which taught managers to hold something back.

questions.text: Mikhail Gorbachev set out to end the Soviet Union when he introduced perestroika and glasnost.
questions.feedback_general: He wanted to repair it. Reform and openness let long-hidden problems and grievances come out. The Soviet parliament formally voted the Union out of existence on December 26, 1991.

questions.text: In 2022, South Korea's GDP per person was $41,321, and North Korea's was $1,569 (2011 international dollars). About how many times larger is South Korea's?
questions.feedback_general: 41,321 divided by 1,569 is about 26.3. North Korea's figure is an estimate, and one comparison cannot prove a rule.

quizzes.title: Lesson 7.01 - Primary Source Exercise
quizzes.description:
"The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

"Society as a whole is more and more splitting up into two great hostile camps, into two great classes directly facing each other."

"... the theory of the Communists may be summed up in the single sentence: Abolition of private property."

"The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie ..."

"Centralisation of credit in the hands of the state ..."

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party (1848), English translation by Samuel Moore, 1888, edited by Frederick Engels. Text from the Marxists Internet Archive. Ellipses mark words left out.

questions.text: The first quotation claims that "all hitherto existing society" shows class struggle. According to the lesson, how should a careful reader test that claim?

answers.text: By assuming it is true because it sounds bold
By asking whether wars between nations, religious divisions, and family rivalries fit neatly into two classes
By counting how many times the word "class" appears
By ignoring the claim because it was written in 1848

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says the authors may have found a real pattern and then stretched it to cover everything. That is a fair thing to say and a fair thing to test.

questions.text: What does the phrase "by degrees" in the fourth quotation tell you?

answers.text: The authors expected the change to happen in a single day
The authors expected only the bourgeoisie to act
The authors did not expect the transfer of capital to happen all at once
The authors wanted the change to be reversed

questions.feedback_general: They said the working class would first need to win political power and then wrest capital from the bourgeoisie gradually.

questions.text: Suppose the Manifesto's prediction had been right. Where would the first revolution have come?

answers.text: In a mostly farming country such as Russia
In a country with no working class

questions.feedback_general: The authors expected revolution first in the most industrial countries. Russia and China, mostly farming countries, were where it actually came.

questions.text: The lesson says the item "Centralisation of credit in the hands of the state" belongs to a larger pattern. Which description fits?

answers.text: It lets markets decide where credit goes
It gives a central authority a decision that markets normally make, raising the question of how that authority would know what to do

questions.feedback_general: Many of the ten measures hand a central authority decisions about where credit goes, what is built, and who works where. That leads to the knowledge question in Lesson 7.04.

questions.text: A wealthy doctor owns no factory and earns her living by selling her services. Where does the Manifesto's scheme place her?

answers.text: Clearly in the bourgeoisie, because she is wealthy
Clearly in the proletariat, because she earns a wage
She does not fit neatly into either box, because the theory sorts people by their relationship to capital, not by how rich they are
In neither, because the Manifesto does not mention classes

questions.feedback_general: The theory is a claim about how people earn a living and what they own.

questions.text: What was the economic complaint of Marx and Engels about the bourgeoisie, given that they admired its productive power?

answers.text: Workers who ran the machines did not share in what the machines produced, and personal worth had been reduced to exchange value

questions.feedback_general: Economists have argued about the claim that workers received only enough to live on for more than a century.

questions.text: The three basic economic questions are what to produce, how to produce, and for whom. Which most directly describes the "for whom" answer in the Soviet command economy?
questions.feedback_general: In a market, wages and prices decide who can buy. In the command economy, the plan assigned goods.

questions.text: The Manifesto lists ten measures. Which item concerns money and banking?

answers.text: Putting credit in the hands of the state through a national bank

questions.feedback_general: Some measures change who owns capital, some change money and banking, some are plans for what to build, and some concern education and taxes.

questions.text: Why did the Bolsheviks gain ground in 1917?

answers.text: The Russian army was winning the war
The weak provisional government could give soldiers and city workers neither peace nor bread

questions.feedback_general: The lesson stresses that nothing was certain. A different decision on the war or on land could have changed the outcome.

questions.text: Under War Communism, armed squads took grain at low fixed prices. What chain of choices does the lesson trace?

answers.text: Farmers grew more, so the cities had more grain
Farmers saw no reward for a surplus, planted less or hid grain, less grain reached cities, and the state requisitioned harder
Farmers moved to cities, so grain prices rose

questions.feedback_general: This is the Module 2 chain: fixed low prices push producers to supply less.

questions.text: The NEP kept which parts of the economy under state control?
questions.feedback_general: Small shops and trade came back, and farmers could sell their surplus after paying the tax.

questions.text: What happened at the Kronstadt naval base in March 1921?

answers.text: Sailors who had once supported the Bolsheviks rebelled over food policy, and the Red Army crushed the rising

questions.feedback_general: Within days, Lenin changed course at the Tenth Party Congress.

questions.text: The famine of 1921 to 1922 is usually estimated to have killed about five million people. Which cause list does the lesson give?

answers.text: War, drought along the Volga River, and the policy itself all played a part

questions.feedback_general: The range of estimates runs wider than five million. Behind the numbers are people with names, families, and villages.

questions.text: Why did Stalin move away from the NEP in 1928?

answers.text: In 1927 the state could not buy enough grain at the low prices it offered, and the cities and army needed food, so he chose force over markets

questions.feedback_general: Bukharin and others argued for keeping the NEP. A different outcome was possible.

questions.text: Why does the lesson note that Nikolai Bukharin argued for keeping the NEP?

answers.text: To show the outcome was not inevitable: a slower, more market-based road to industry existed

questions.feedback_general: We cannot know how that road would have gone, but we can see that it existed.

questions.text: Estimates of industrial growth under the first Five-Year Plan range from about 50 percent to 118 percent. What does the lesson say this gap shows?

answers.text: Counting can depend on method, and when the people who run a system also report on it, numbers may reflect what the system wants to hear

questions.feedback_general: Historians describe 1930 as an era of exaggeration in the official claims.

questions.text: A manager meets a target, and the target is then raised. What does the lesson say this teaches the manager?

answers.text: To exceed every target by as much as possible

questions.feedback_general: Targets were often raised after they were met, according to the historian Sheila Fitzpatrick.

questions.text: The Soviet government used the word kulak for better-off farmers. According to the lesson, how did the label function?

answers.text: It was stretched to cover anyone who resisted

questions.feedback_general: One estimate counts about 3.5 million people stripped of their property between 1929 and 1931.

questions.text: Some farmers slaughtered their own animals rather than hand them over. What does the lesson say this shows about incentives?

answers.text: If the reward for keeping something is taken away, people may destroy it instead

questions.feedback_general: A farmer who cannot keep the reward for raising an animal may decide that eating it is the better option.

questions.text: The famine of 1932 to 1933 is estimated to have killed how many people?

answers.text: About 3 million to nearly 9 million, depending on the historian and how deaths are counted

questions.feedback_general: The government denied the famine and refused foreign aid. The lesson asks you to carry the weight of the number, not push it away.

questions.text: The lesson says that "when a system cannot hear bad news," mistakes grow. Why does a market hear bad news more easily?

answers.text: Prices rise, profits fall, and firms change what they do, without anyone having to report failure upward

questions.feedback_general: In a command economy, reports flow up and orders flow down, and when reporting failure is dangerous, the center loses its eyes.

questions.text: Von Mises argued in 1920 that planners lacking real market prices for tools and materials:
questions.feedback_general: Hayek built on a related idea: that prices carry dispersed knowledge no single mind can hold.

questions.text: A computer can process more data than any 1930s planner could. How does the lesson treat this question?

answers.text: It says the knowledge problem is solved
It says computers cannot be used in economics
It says economists disagree: some think the problem is now smaller, while others argue that the most useful knowledge is local, changing, and often unspoken
It says nobody has considered the question

questions.feedback_general: The lesson asks you to be ready to defend whichever side you find stronger.

questions.text: Which row of the lesson's incentive table matches its pattern?

answers.text: NEP: no reward for a surplus, so farmers hid grain
War Communism: no reward for a surplus, so farmers planted less or hid grain; NEP: a tax and the right to sell the rest, so output recovered
Five-Year Plan: a reward for serving buyers

questions.feedback_general: The pattern repeats across the Soviet record: output responds to whether effort is rewarded.

questions.text: What did Gorbachev's reforms of perestroika and glasnost mean?

answers.text: Perestroika meant restructuring the economy, and glasnost meant allowing more public discussion and criticism

questions.feedback_general: Reform and openness did not rescue the system; they let long-hidden problems and grievances come out.

questions.text: On which dates did the Soviet Union end, according to the lesson?

answers.text: Only on December 8, 1991, when it was dissolved
The Belovezha Accords on December 8, Gorbachev's resignation on December 25, and the parliament's vote dissolving the Union on December 26, 1991

questions.feedback_general: The lesson says historians do not agree on one cause: a slow, wasteful economy, the cost of the arms race and a war in Afghanistan, falling oil prices, and national feeling in the republics all appear.

questions.text: Why is the Korean comparison strong evidence but not proof?

answers.text: North Korea's figure is an estimate, many things beyond property rights differ, and one comparison cannot prove a rule

questions.feedback_general: The two countries also fought a destructive war and received different foreign help. Much of the peninsula's heavy industry sat in the north in 1945, which makes the gap more striking.

questions.text: Which statement summarizes the link between property rights and prosperity that the lesson draws?

answers.text: Where protections are weak, people work and invest more
Where people can own what they produce and enforce contracts, they tend to work, invest, and take risks
Property rights matter only in the United States
Property rights have no effect on incentives

questions.feedback_general: The Korean gap, the Soviet harvests, and the NEP rebound all point the same way.

questions.text: How does the lesson judge the command economy against the first-order economic problem?

answers.text: It was a clear failure on every measure

It showed real results in defense and heavy industry for a time, but on producing and distributing enough that the whole population prospers the evidence is poor, though that does not mean markets are perfect

questions.feedback_general: Markets produce unequal outcomes and costs that fall on third parties, and Marx's question about whether working people share in a society's wealth is still worth asking.

questions.text: A one-year Treasury bill has a face value of $1,000. An investor pays $950 for it. About what is the yield?
questions.feedback_general: The investor earns $1,000 minus $950, which is $50. The yield is $50 divided by the $950 paid, about 5.26 percent. Dividing by $1,000 would be the wrong base.

questions.text: A year after you bought a 10-year note paying 4 percent, new notes are being sold that pay 5 percent. If you want to sell your old note, what will probably happen to its price?

answers.text: It will fall, so that the buyer's yield can compete with the new notes

questions.feedback_general: The payments on the old note are fixed. To compete, its price must fall, and the yield for the person who buys it rises. Price and yield move opposite ways.

questions.text: A Treasury bill pays interest every six months.
questions.feedback_general: A bill pays no regular interest. You buy it for less than face value and receive the full face value at maturity. Notes and bonds pay interest every six months.

questions.text: Why is the Treasury yield called a benchmark?

answers.text: It is the highest rate in the economy
Other lenders start from it and add something for risk

questions.feedback_general: Treasuries are among the safest investments, backed by the taxing power of the government. Anyone riskier has to offer more.

questions.text: What problem were TIPS (inflation-protected securities) designed to answer?

answers.text: Inflation quietly shrinking what a fixed payment can buy, since the principal rises with the Consumer Price Index

questions.feedback_general: A saver who cares about buying power, not just dollars, has a reason to look at them.

questions.text: Why does fractional-reserve banking make bank runs possible?

answers.text: Banks keep every deposit in the vault
Banks keep only a fraction as reserves and lend the rest, so they cannot pay everyone at once

questions.feedback_general: A bank can pay back depositors on a normal day. It cannot pay all of them at once, because most of the money is out in loans.

questions.text: In the textbook story, banks keep a fixed fraction of each deposit as reserves. If that fraction were 20 percent, the most a $1,000 deposit could support in total deposits is:
questions.feedback_general: $1,000 divided by 0.20 is $5,000. A higher reserve ratio holds back more of each deposit, so the total is lower.

questions.text: As of March 26, 2020, the Federal Reserve Board set reserve requirement ratios at zero percent.
questions.feedback_general: The Board said this followed "the shift to an ample reserves regime." Banks are still limited by capital rules, by the need to find borrowers who will repay, and by the cost of lending that the Fed's rate decisions change.

questions.text: Which two tools does the lesson say do most of the Fed's work today?

answers.text: Reserve requirements and the discount window only
Open market operations and the interest the Fed pays banks on reserves

questions.feedback_general: A bank has little reason to lend reserves to another bank for less than the Fed pays it to leave them there, so that rate acts as a floor.

questions.text: What does the Federal Open Market Committee vote on?

answers.text: A target range for the federal funds rate

questions.feedback_general: The Fed then uses its tools to keep the actual rate inside that range. The rate ripples out to other rates.

questions.text: On the sample $162,000 loan at 3.875 percent, the first monthly payment is $761.78. About how much of that first payment is interest?
questions.feedback_general: Interest is charged on the full balance: $162,000 times the monthly rate 0.0032292 is about $523.13. The remaining $238.65 reduces the principal.

questions.text: Which factor that sets your rate is controlled by markets and the Fed, not by you?
questions.feedback_general: You cannot control the benchmark, but you can control a lot of what is added to it.

questions.text: The annual percentage rate (APR) on a loan is always the same as its interest rate.
questions.feedback_general: The APR folds in the loan's fees and other costs. On the sample form, the interest rate is 3.875 percent and the APR is 4.274 percent.

questions.text: What is an escrow account?

answers.text: A savings account the borrower may withdraw from anytime
An account where the lender holds part of your payment to pay your property taxes and homeowner's insurance

questions.feedback_general: In the sample, escrow is $206 a month. It protects the lender, since an unpaid tax bill can put a claim on the house.

questions.text: Whom does private mortgage insurance protect?

answers.text: The borrower, if the house loses value
The lender, if the borrower stops paying

questions.feedback_general: Lenders often require it when the down payment is small. In the sample it adds $82 a month for the first seven years.

questions.text: On the sample loan, the tipping point comes at payment number 147. What does that mean?

answers.text: It is the first payment in which more than half goes to principal

questions.feedback_general: In payment 146, interest is still ahead by two cents. In payment 147, principal is ahead: $382.11 against $379.67. That is 12 years and 3 months into the loan.

questions.text: After five years of payments on the $162,000 loan, about how much of the original loan is still owed?
questions.feedback_general: The balance after 60 payments is $146,227.42, about 90.3 percent of $162,000. If you sell after five years, the sale price has to cover that before you keep any profit.

questions.text: Compared with the 30-year loan at the same rate, a 15-year loan has:

answers.text: A lower payment and lower total interest
A higher payment and much lower total interest
A lower payment and higher total interest
The same payment and the same interest

questions.feedback_general: The monthly payment goes from $761.78 to $1,188.17, but total interest falls from $112,240.80 to $51,870.60. You owe the balance for fewer months.

questions.text: A refinance costs $2,400 and lowers the monthly payment by $40. How many months does it take to break even?
questions.feedback_general: Divide the cost by the monthly savings: $2,400 divided by $40 is 60 months. If you expect to move or pay off the loan sooner, you lose money by refinancing.

questions.text: What does the total cost of credit include?

answers.text: The price of the thing you are buying
Interest plus required fees and insurance, not the amount borrowed

questions.feedback_general: Decide what belongs by asking: would I pay this if I did not need to borrow?

quizzes.title: Lesson 8.02 - Primary Source Exercise
quizzes.description:
"In support of these goals, the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent and anticipates that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate."

"Inflation remains elevated, reflecting supply and demand imbalances related to the pandemic, higher energy prices, and broader price pressures."

Federal Reserve, "Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement," March 16, 2022. federalreserve.gov.

questions.text: What did the Committee decide to do?

answers.text: Raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/4 to 1/2 percent

questions.feedback_general: This ended a period, since March 2020, in which the range had been held near zero.

questions.text: The statement also says the Committee "anticipates that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate." Why does that signal matter?

answers.text: It has no effect until the next meeting
It shapes what banks and borrowers expect and do before anything else happens

questions.feedback_general: People adjust to what they expect the Fed to do, so the forecast itself changes behavior.

questions.text: Which cause of elevated inflation does the statement name?
questions.feedback_general: The statement lists supply and demand imbalances related to the pandemic, higher energy prices, and broader price pressures.

questions.text: James Bullard dissented, preferring a 0.5 percentage point increase to a range of 1/2 to 3/4 percent. Compared with what the Committee chose, his preference would have been:

answers.text: A larger and faster increase in rates

questions.feedback_general: He did not oppose raising rates. He wanted a bigger step. Even the experts disagreed about how fast to go.

quizzes.title: Lesson 8.03 - Primary Source Exercise
quizzes.description:
"Annual Percentage Rate (APR) 4.274%. Your costs over the loan term expressed as a rate. This is not your interest rate."

"In 5 Years: $56,582. Total you will have paid in principal, interest, mortgage insurance, and loan costs. $15,773. Principal you will have paid off."

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, sample Loan Estimate H-24(B), Fixed Rate Loan, February 7, 2014 (page 3, "Comparisons"). The names and lender on the sample are fictional.

questions.text: The sample's interest rate is 3.875 percent, and its APR is 4.274 percent. Why is the APR higher?

answers.text: The APR expresses the loan's costs over its term as a rate, so it includes fees as well as interest

questions.feedback_general: The form says so in one sentence: the APR is "not your interest rate."

questions.text: Roughly what share of the $56,582 paid over five years went to reduce principal?
questions.feedback_general: $15,773 divided by $56,582 is about 0.279, or about 28 percent. The rest went to interest, mortgage insurance, and loan costs.

questions.text: Suppose two lenders offer the same loan, and one has a lower interest rate but a much higher APR. What should a careful borrower conclude?

answers.text: The lower-rate lender probably charges higher fees, so the other loan may cost less overall, and the borrower should ask why
The higher APR means a lower monthly payment

questions.feedback_general: If one lender has a lower rate and a much higher APR, ask why. A careful borrower asks until the answers make sense.

questions.text: Why did so little of the five-year total go to principal?

answers.text: Principal is not repaid until the last year
Early payments on an amortized loan are mostly interest, and the total also includes mortgage insurance and loan costs

questions.feedback_general: Interest is charged on the balance you still owe, so it is largest at the beginning.

questions.text: A one-year Treasury bill with a $1,000 face value sells for $940. What is the approximate yield?
questions.feedback_general: $1,000 minus $940 is $60, and $60 divided by $940 is about 6.38 percent.

questions.text: If investors suddenly want the safety of Treasury securities and bid up their price, what happens to yields?
questions.feedback_general: The payoff at maturity is fixed, so a higher price means a lower return on the money you put in.

questions.text: Which statement describes the relationship between a Treasury yield and a bank's mortgage rate?

answers.text: Lenders start from the benchmark yield for a similar maturity and add a premium for risk
Mortgage rates are set by the Treasury
The mortgage rate is always lower than the Treasury yield

questions.feedback_general: Mortgage rates and long-term Treasury yields tend to move in the same direction over time.

questions.text: A lender builds a rate this way: a 4.0 percent benchmark, plus 0.5 percentage points for the long term, plus 1.0 percentage point for the borrower's late payments. What rate does it ask?
questions.feedback_general: 4.0 plus 0.5 plus 1.0 is 5.5 percent. A borrower with a spotless history would see the credit add-on shrink or disappear.

questions.text: Which borrower is likely to pay the highest rate, according to the lesson's risk ladder?
questions.feedback_general: Risk rises along the ladder, and so does the rate a lender asks, because repayment is least certain for the weak-credit borrower.

questions.text: When the government runs a deficit, how does it cover the gap?

answers.text: By selling Treasury securities, which are auctioned to investors

questions.feedback_general: The price is set by buyers and sellers, not by a government order. Over time the interest on this borrowing becomes a cost in the budget.

questions.text: Which type of Treasury security pays interest every six months and returns face value in 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years?
questions.feedback_general: Bills run 4 to 52 weeks and pay no regular interest. Bonds run 20 or 30 years.

questions.text: With a reserve ratio of 10 percent, what is the most that a $1,000 deposit can support in total deposits?
questions.feedback_general: $1,000 divided by 0.10 is $10,000. Lending creates money: the new deposits are real spending power that did not exist before the loans.

questions.text: Since March 26, 2020, what has been the required reserve ratio set by the Federal Reserve Board?
questions.feedback_general: The textbook multiplier story still shows how lending creates deposits, but it is no longer the rule that limits banks.

questions.text: What does the Fed's dual mandate consist of?

answers.text: High interest rates and a strong dollar

questions.feedback_general: The two goals can pull against each other. Lower rates help employment but can push prices up, and higher rates cool prices but can slow hiring.

questions.text: Which sequence correctly traces how an FOMC rate increase reaches borrowers?

answers.text: Banks lower their loan rates, borrowing rises, prices rise
The target range rises, banks pay more for short-term money, banks raise loan rates, borrowing costs more, spending cools
The Treasury sets bank rates, then borrowers set prices
Prices fall first, then the FOMC meets

questions.feedback_general: A rate decision that looks small in the news is large when multiplied across a lifetime of borrowing.

questions.text: On a $162,000 30-year loan, the monthly payment rises from $761.78 at 3.875 percent to $857.32 at 4.875 percent. About how much does one percentage point add each month?
questions.feedback_general: $857.32 minus $761.78 is $95.54. Over 360 months that is tens of thousands of dollars.

questions.text: Why do variable-rate loans respond quickly when the Fed changes course?

answers.text: Their rates move up and down with a benchmark

questions.feedback_general: A fixed-rate loan locks in the rate you were given. Fixed rates are usually a little higher at the start in exchange for certainty.

questions.text: A borrower takes a $200,000 loan at 6 percent for 30 years. The monthly payment is $1,199.10. How much of the first payment is interest?
questions.feedback_general: The monthly rate is 0.06 divided by 12, or 0.005. Interest is $200,000 times 0.005, or $1,000.00. The other $199.10 reduces the principal.

questions.text: For that same $200,000 loan, which is closest to the total interest paid over 30 years?
questions.feedback_general: 360 payments of $1,199.10 total $431,676. Subtract the $200,000 borrowed, and the interest is about $231,700. Total payments are about 2.16 times what was borrowed.

questions.text: Why does the interest part of each payment shrink over time on an amortized loan?

answers.text: The lender lowers the rate each year
Interest is charged on the balance still owed, which gets smaller

questions.feedback_general: The payment is fixed, so as interest shrinks, the part left over for principal grows. Early payments are mostly interest.

questions.text: Which statement about credit scores is supported by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, as quoted in the lesson?

answers.text: There is exactly one score for every person
Most scores run from 300 to 850, and you do not have just one score, since it can vary by model, by kind of loan, and by date

questions.feedback_general: The Bureau calls a score "a prediction of your credit behavior."

questions.text: In the sample Loan Estimate, the home costs $180,000 and the loan is $162,000. What percent is the down payment?
questions.feedback_general: The down payment is $18,000, which is 10 percent of $180,000. A bigger down payment lowers the lender's risk.

questions.text: How is the sample's "Estimated Cash to Close" of $16,054 built?

answers.text: Closing costs of $8,054 plus the $18,000 down payment, minus the $10,000 deposit already paid

questions.feedback_general: $8,054 plus $18,000 is $26,054, minus $10,000 is $16,054. Closing costs are often forgotten when families plan a purchase.

questions.text: In the sample, the projected monthly payment falls from $1,050 in years 1 to 7 to $968 in years 8 to 30. Why?

answers.text: The mortgage insurance of $82 a month ends

questions.feedback_general: $1,050 minus $82 is $968. Principal and interest ($761.78) and escrow ($206) continue.

questions.text: The Total Interest Percentage on the sample form (69.45 percent) differs slightly from a straight calculation of total interest divided by the loan amount (about 69.3 percent). What does the lesson recommend?

answers.text: Report the small gap honestly, and use that line only to compare loans on the same form

questions.feedback_general: When two honest numbers disagree slightly, say so and keep working, rather than pretending they match.

questions.text: A student compares a 48-month and a 60-month car loan for $20,000 at 6 percent. The 48-month total interest is $2,545.60, and the 60-month total is $3,199.60. How much more interest does the longer loan cost?
questions.feedback_general: $3,199.60 minus $2,545.60 is $654.00. The longer loan is easier on the monthly budget but keeps her in debt another year while the car loses value.

questions.text: Why are extra payments especially powerful early in a loan?

answers.text: They reduce the principal while it is large, so less interest builds up afterward

questions.feedback_general: Adding $100 to every payment on the sample loan pays it off in 290 months instead of 360, saving about $24,576 in interest. Check for a prepayment penalty first.

questions.text: The sample loan's total cost of credit comes to about $124,801. Which items add up to it?

answers.text: The $180,000 sale price plus the $18,000 down payment
Interest of $112,240.80, loan costs of $5,672, and mortgage insurance of $6,888 (82 times 84)

questions.feedback_general: Taxes and homeowner's insurance are real costs but not costs of credit. The test is: would I pay this if I did not need to borrow?

questions.text: Which step in the seven-step credit plan helps protect you if your income falls or a variable rate rises?
questions.feedback_general: The steps are purpose, price and down payment, rate, term, total cost of credit, budget, and risks. They do not guarantee a good result, but they make a bad surprise far less likely.

questions.text: In one day, Country X can produce either 6 cars or 12 televisions, and Country Y can produce either 2 cars or 8 televisions. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Country Y has an absolute advantage in both goods
Country X has the comparative advantage in cars, and Country Y has the comparative advantage in televisions
Country X has the comparative advantage in both goods

questions.feedback_general: Country X gives up 2 televisions per car, and Country Y gives up 4. X has the lower opportunity cost of cars. Y gives up only 0.25 car per television, against 0.5 for X, so Y has the comparative advantage in televisions, even though X produces more of both.

questions.text: Why can a country gain from trade even if it has no absolute advantage in anything?

answers.text: It can specialize where its opportunity cost is lowest, and both countries end up with more

questions.feedback_general: Comparative advantage means being the "least bad" at something relative to your own alternatives.

questions.text: An importer pays a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on a $200 imported good. How much is the tariff?
questions.feedback_general: Ad valorem means "according to value": 10 percent of $200 is $20. A specific tariff is a flat dollar amount per unit.

questions.text: A country restricts imports of medical supplies so it never depends on a rival for them. Which rationale for trade barriers is this?
questions.feedback_general: National security (oil, food, medical supplies) and foreign policy (sanctions, embargoes) are rationales alongside protecting infant industries.

questions.text: In the circular flow model, where do firms get the land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship they use to produce?
questions.feedback_general: Households supply the factors of production and earn wages, rent, interest, and profit. They then spend that income in the product market.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call the Korean peninsula the clearest "natural experiment"?

answers.text: The two countries began with very different cultures
They started in 1945 with the same population, culture, and history, so the later gap isolates the effect of economic and legal systems
North Korea began with far more people

questions.feedback_general: Because almost everything else started out the same, the comparison isolates institutions and property rights.

questions.text: What is "Dutch disease"?

answers.text: A commodity boom that raises a currency's value and harms a country's other industries

questions.feedback_general: Resource-rich developing nations can face it, which is why resource wealth does not guarantee growth.

questions.text: Adam Smith's pin factory illustrates which idea?
questions.feedback_general: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Smith also described people pursuing self-interest through markets and serving society's needs too.

questions.text: Which school argued that wages and prices are "sticky" and slow to adjust, leaving real room for policy to matter?
questions.feedback_general: The new classical school stressed rational expectations. New Keynesians stressed stickiness.

questions.text: The lesson calls installment credit a tool, not a wicked thing. What rule does the tool have built in?

answers.text: Every payment owed next year comes out of next year's income, and if that income stops, the payments do not
Lenders must lower payments in a downturn

questions.feedback_general: In the 1920s millions of households took on payments at once, and nobody had tested what would happen if paychecks shrank.

questions.text: Machines let one farmer plow more land, and more wheat reached the market, so wheat prices fell. What did farmers do next, according to the lesson?

answers.text: Plowed even more land to earn the same income, so the native grass that held the soil was lost

questions.feedback_general: Every single decision made sense. Together they stripped the Plains of its grass.

questions.text: Why did the closing of the Bank of United States in December 1930 matter?

answers.text: It was a small rural bank with no effect
It was the fourth-largest bank in New York City, and its closing shook trust in banks across the country

questions.feedback_general: Fear spread faster than facts, and depositors began to worry even about banks that were perfectly healthy.

questions.text: The Dow closed at 41.22 on July 8, 1932. About how far below its September 1929 peak of 381.17 was that?
questions.feedback_general: 41.22 divided by 381.17 is about 0.108, so the Dow was about 89 percent below its peak. A person who put $1,000 into the average stock in September 1929 would have had roughly $110 by the summer of 1932.

questions.text: What is a "discouraged worker"?

answers.text: A worker who has a job but dislikes it
A person who is out of work and has stopped looking, so is not counted as unemployed
A worker who quit to start a business

questions.feedback_general: In a deep downturn some people stop looking because there is nothing to find, so even a careful count can miss part of the damage.

questions.text: In the spiral described in Lesson 6.03, what comes right after businesses cut costs because falling prices squeeze profits?

answers.text: More workers are laid off, which cuts spending again

questions.feedback_general: Then the loop starts again from the top, which is why economists fear a steady fall in prices.

questions.text: The Soil Conservation Service created in 1935 exists today under which name?
questions.feedback_general: Congress adopted the new name in 1994.

questions.text: The lesson describes a "sunk-cost trap" for a farm family deciding whether to leave. What is it?

answers.text: The more you have already put into a farm, the harder it feels to walk away, though money already spent is gone either way
Banks will not allow families to leave

questions.feedback_general: A good decision looks forward. That is easy to say and very hard to do.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say Hoover was "following the textbook of his day"?

answers.text: A balanced budget, even in hard times, was widely held as sound policy in 1932, and Keynes's major book arguing the opposite did not appear until 1936

questions.feedback_general: Whether the textbook was right is what the Depression put to the test.

questions.text: When did the FDIC begin insuring deposits, and for how much per depositor at the start?

answers.text: January 1, 1934, up to $2,500, raised to $5,000 in July 1934

questions.feedback_general: The Banking Act of 1933, often called Glass-Steagall, created the FDIC.

questions.text: On what ground did the Supreme Court hold part of the NIRA unconstitutional in Schechter (1935)?

answers.text: It gave too much lawmaking power to the executive branch, and Congress lacked authority over a small local business

questions.feedback_general: The vote was unanimous, and Chief Justice Hughes wrote the opinion.

questions.text: What does the lesson conclude about the cause of the 1937 recession?

answers.text: Economists agree it was caused by the FDIC
It is still debated: one argument blames the Fed's doubling of reserve requirements, while other economists found the new rules did not bind most banks
It was caused only by the AAA

questions.feedback_general: The cause is not settled. The lesson asks you to be confident of what is documented and honest about what is not.

questions.text: "Resolved personal worth into exchange value." What does the Manifesto mean by this charge against the bourgeoisie?

answers.text: Everything, including a worker's time and effort, was reduced to a price

questions.feedback_general: The authors admired the bourgeoisie's productive power, but they charged that workers did not share in what the machines produced.

questions.text: The Manifesto's measures 7, 8, and 9 (state-owned factories and a common plan, required work and labor armies, and combining farming with manufacturing) are mainly examples of which kind of change?
questions.feedback_general: The lesson sorts the ten measures into ownership of capital, taxation, money and banking, planning, and education. The pattern is that a central authority takes decisions that markets normally make.

questions.text: Which description of Russia in 1917 matches the lesson?

answers.text: A mostly farming country, with large factories only in cities such as Petrograd and Moscow

questions.feedback_general: A strict reading of the Manifesto would have told Lenin to wait. He argued that a small, disciplined party could lead city workers and win farmers' support.

questions.text: After taking power, which actions did the Bolsheviks take in their first months?

answers.text: They disbanded the secret police and held elections
They created the Cheka (secret police) and broke up the elected assembly after a single meeting

questions.feedback_general: They made peace with Germany in March 1918, and then a civil war began between the Reds and the Whites.

questions.text: Why were Soviet planners' reports on output often unreliable?

answers.text: The people who ran the system also reported on it, so numbers could reflect what the system wanted to hear

questions.feedback_general: Historians describe 1930 as an era of exaggeration in the official claims.

questions.text: What was the lesson's balanced judgment of the Five-Year Plan?

answers.text: The industrial base it built helped the Soviet Union survive the 1941 German invasion, but consumer goods fell sharply and food grew scarce

questions.feedback_general: On the first-order economic problem, producing and distributing enough that the whole population prospers, the record is poor.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call a price "a message"?

answers.text: A price carries knowledge from people who have it to people who need it, without telling them why

questions.feedback_general: The buyer in the tin example only needs to see that the price has risen.

questions.text: Which pair appears among the causes of the Soviet collapse that historians cite in the lesson?

answers.text: The cost of the arms race and a long war in Afghanistan, together with falling oil prices in the 1980s
A harvest of record size and a free press
A new tsar and a civil war

questions.feedback_general: Historians do not agree on a single cause. National feeling in the republics and particular decisions also appear.

questions.text: The lesson adds that much of the Korean peninsula's heavy industry sat in the north in 1945. What does that fact do to the comparison of the two Koreas?

answers.text: It weakens the case that South Korea's GDP per person is higher
It makes the gap more striking, because the north started with the advantage
It proves property rights do not matter
It shows North Korea's figure is exact

questions.feedback_general: The lesson still cautions that North Korea's figure is an estimate and that one comparison cannot prove a rule.

questions.text: A one-year Treasury bill with a $1,000 face value sells for $970. About what is the yield?
questions.feedback_general: $1,000 minus $970 is $30, and $30 divided by $970 is about 3.09 percent. Dividing by the face value would give 3.00 percent, which is the wrong base.

questions.text: An offer promises a high return with no risk. According to the lesson, how should you react?

answers.text: Accept it, since high returns are good
With suspicion, because return and risk travel together

questions.feedback_general: Honesty about this tradeoff is a mark of a trustworthy adviser, and of a trustworthy person managing their own money.

questions.text: Why does the lesson say the textbook reserve-multiplier story is no longer the rule that limits bank lending?

answers.text: The required reserve ratio has been zero since March 26, 2020, so capital rules, finding borrowers who will repay, and the cost of lending now do more of the limiting

questions.feedback_general: The story still shows how lending creates deposits.

questions.text: Why does the interest the Fed pays on reserves act as a floor under short-term rates?

answers.text: Banks must lend reserves to the Treasury
The Fed sets every bank's loan rate
A bank has little reason to lend reserves to another bank for less than the Fed pays it to leave them there

questions.feedback_general: When the Fed raises that rate, other short-term rates tend to follow.

questions.text: A $162,000, 30-year loan costs $672.13 a month at 2.875 percent and $958.29 at 5.875 percent. How much more is the monthly payment at the higher rate?
questions.feedback_general: $958.29 minus $672.13 is $286.16 a month, across 360 months more than $100,000.

questions.text: On the Loan Estimate, "Balloon Payment: No" means:

answers.text: There is no large lump-sum payment due at the end of the loan

questions.feedback_general: A balloon payment is a large lump sum due at maturity.

questions.text: The sample form's prepayment penalty is "as high as $3,240" in the first two years on a $162,000 loan. What does the lesson say that is?

answers.text: 2 percent of the balance for two years

questions.feedback_general: Two percent of $162,000 is $3,240. A borrower should know exactly what the lender counts as a penalty before sending extra money.

questions.text: How does the lesson say to use the Loan Estimate when shopping?

answers.text: Pick the lender with the lowest advertised rate
Get Loan Estimates for the same loan from at least two lenders, and compare the rate, APR, monthly payment, cash to close, and any penalty side by side

questions.feedback_general: If one lender has a lower rate and a much higher APR, ask why.

questions.text: The sample loan with 20 percent down ($36,000 down, $144,000 borrowed) has a payment of $677.14. How much less is that per month than the base case of $761.78?
questions.feedback_general: $761.78 minus $677.14 is $84.64. Total interest also falls, from $112,240.80 to $99,770.40.

questions.text: A refinance costs $4,500 and lowers the monthly payment by $75. How many months does it take to break even?
questions.feedback_general: $4,500 divided by $75 is 60 months. If you expect to move or pay off the loan sooner, refinancing loses money.

questions.text: Tickets to a popular concert sell out in minutes because far more people want them than there are seats. Which idea does this illustrate?
questions.feedback_general: Scarcity means there is never enough of everything to satisfy every possible use for it. It is a microeconomic example, since it concerns one market.

questions.text: Two classmates face the same choice, a concert ticket or saving for a phone, and rationally choose differently. Why?

answers.text: Opportunity cost does not exist for students
They place different utility on each option

questions.feedback_general: Utility is the satisfaction a person gets from a good, service, or choice. Cost-benefit analysis weighs what is gained against what is lost.

questions.text: The lesson calls land a "gift of nature." Which statement is also true of land?
questions.feedback_general: Land covers every natural resource from the Earth: soil, forests, minerals, fossil fuels, sunlight, wind, and water.

questions.text: Which features describe a traditional economy?

answers.text: Custom passed down through generations, subsistence production, and barter

questions.feedback_general: It is the oldest system. It offers strong social cohesion, but little technological change.

questions.text: Which event shifts the supply curve for a good to the right?
questions.feedback_general: New technology means more at every price. A drought or a new tax shifts supply left, and a rise in income shifts demand right.

questions.text: Why is a firm in perfect competition called a "price taker"?

answers.text: There are many small firms selling an identical product, so no single firm can influence the price

questions.feedback_general: Free entry and exit push long-run economic profit toward zero.

questions.text: What risk does the lesson attach to relying on price competition alone?

answers.text: It compresses profit margins and can push firms toward under-investment in quality or workers

questions.feedback_general: Nonprice competition builds loyalty that survives a price increase, but it requires sustained investment.

questions.text: What is "double taxation" of a corporation?

answers.text: A tax on both the owner and the manager
The corporation pays tax on its profits, and shareholders pay tax again on the dividends

questions.feedback_general: An LLC, a pass-through entity, avoids it.

questions.text: An airline's marginal cost for one more passenger on a flight already scheduled is very low. What does that explain?

answers.text: Why last-minute discount fares can still be profitable

questions.feedback_general: Fuel and crew are already paid for, so the extra passenger adds little cost.

questions.text: Zimbabwe and Venezuela both suffered hyperinflation. Which characteristic of good money broke down?
questions.feedback_general: Unlimited money collapses in value.

questions.text: Why do Federal Reserve decisions reverberate around the world?

answers.text: The dollar is the world's primary reserve currency, so higher U.S. rates strengthen the dollar and raise repayment costs for countries with dollar debt
Every country uses the federal funds rate

questions.feedback_general: The Fed's mandate is officially domestic, but its reach is de facto global.

questions.text: What did the "taper tantrum" refer to?

answers.text: Capital that had flowed into emerging markets rushing back to the United States when the Fed raised rates after a period of low rates

questions.feedback_general: Such shifts can trigger balance-of-payments crises that require help from the International Monetary Fund.

questions.text: Why would a saver choose a Certificate of Deposit over a regular savings account?

answers.text: A CD has no risk and no term
A CD pays a slightly higher rate in exchange for locking funds up for a set term

questions.feedback_general: CDs trade liquidity for a higher rate.

questions.text: Financial experts generally recommend keeping total monthly debt payments below what share of income?
questions.feedback_general: This is a guideline for borrowing within your means. A budget also has to be reviewed monthly, not just built once.

questions.text: Which are the three goals of fiscal policy in the lesson?

answers.text: Price stability, full employment, and sustainable growth

questions.feedback_general: The trade-off across all three is public debt.

questions.text: What is "crowding out"?

answers.text: Government spending that creates too many jobs
Heavy government borrowing raising interest rates by competing with households and businesses for credit

questions.feedback_general: Crowding out can make mortgages and business loans more expensive.

questions.text: What happened in Weimar Germany in the 1920s, according to the lesson?

answers.text: Prices doubled every few days, savings evaporated, and people resorted to barter or foreign currency
The government raised interest rates to 15 percent

questions.feedback_general: This is hyperinflation, a different order of magnitude from high inflation.

questions.text: What is a Pigovian tax?

answers.text: A tax on an activity that creates a negative externality, meant to make the producer pay something closer to the true social cost
A tax on sales to the poor

questions.feedback_general: Cap-and-trade systems and carbon taxes work on a similar principle.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call education a positive externality?

answers.text: An educated population raises innovation and civic participation well beyond any individual graduate

questions.feedback_general: That is the economic case for public investment in schools.

questions.text: Country P can make 20 shirts or 10 phones per day. Country Q can make 10 shirts or 8 phones per day. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Country P has the comparative advantage in phones
Country Q has the comparative advantage in phones, even though P has an absolute advantage in both goods
Country Q has an absolute advantage in shirts

questions.feedback_general: P gives up 2 shirts per phone, and Q gives up 1.25. Q has the lower opportunity cost of phones.

questions.text: The USMCA replaced NAFTA. Which countries are its members?
questions.feedback_general: It is a trade agreement, and it is a shallower form of integration than the European Union.

questions.text: What is the purpose of transfer payments such as unemployment insurance in the circular flow?

answers.text: To support households whose private income falls short

questions.feedback_general: They are not payment for land, labor, or capital.

questions.text: What do Bangladesh and Rwanda show?

answers.text: Real economic progress is possible even without abundant natural resources

questions.feedback_general: The lesson cites Bangladesh's export industries and Rwanda's governance reform.

questions.text: What is stagflation, and why did it challenge the prevailing schools?

answers.text: Falling prices and low unemployment, which supported Keynes
High unemployment and high inflation at once, which neither Keynesians nor monetarists could fix together
A rapid asset price rise and a collapse

questions.feedback_general: The 1970s embarrassed both schools and pushed the new classical, New Keynesian, and Austrian schools forward.

questions.text: The lesson says a weakening of habits of prudence across a society leaves less room to absorb a shock. How does it treat the claim that this was the main cause of the Depression?

answers.text: It says economists still argue about it, and it returns to the debate honestly in Lesson 6.06

questions.feedback_general: A farmer who borrowed to feed his family was not a speculator. The point is about habits across a whole society.

questions.text: The Federal Reserve's own history reports that the Dow closed at 381.17 on September 3, 1929. According to the lesson, the Dow did not climb back to that high until:
questions.feedback_general: It reached a low of 41.22 on July 8, 1932.

questions.text: Which place did the lesson use as an example of unemployment reaching 35.8 percent, showing that national figures hide differences?
questions.feedback_general: A town that depended on one mine or one factory could lose nearly everything at once.

questions.text: Why was the effect of the drought on Plains soil so severe, according to the lesson?

answers.text: Plowing had removed the native grass whose roots held the soil, so when the drought came the wind could lift the topsoil
The Soil Conservation Service plowed too deeply

questions.feedback_general: The prairie had survived dry years for thousands of years. What changed was what lay on top of the ground.

questions.text: Section 7(a) of the National Industrial Recovery Act gave workers the right to:

answers.text: Join unions and take part in collective bargaining

questions.feedback_general: Collective bargaining means bargaining as a group with the employer.

questions.text: Which caution does the lesson attach to Christina Romer's finding that monetary expansion explains nearly all recovery before 1942?

answers.text: It is one economist's analysis and does not mean spending did nothing, and critics argue the usual measures may understate fiscal effects

questions.feedback_general: The lesson does not ask you to choose a winner. It shows how a careful person holds an open question.

questions.text: In "the history of all hitherto existing society," what does "hitherto" mean?
questions.feedback_general: The authors claim that if you look at any society in recorded history, you will find groups pulling against each other.

questions.text: Why did Lenin's party gain from the provisional government's decision to stay in the war?

answers.text: Soldiers and city workers wanted peace and bread, and the government could not provide either

questions.feedback_general: The Bolsheviks promised "Peace, land, and bread."

questions.text: Why did Stalin's plan put heavy industry first?

answers.text: The reasoning was that an industrial base would make the country strong, fast, and the cost was a sharp fall in consumer goods

questions.feedback_general: Heavy industry means steel, coal, electric power, and machines.

questions.text: Why are GDP-per-person figures for the two Koreas given in "2011 international dollars"?

answers.text: Because the United States rules require it
The unit adjusts for what money can actually buy in each place
Because the Korean won has no value
Because it is the only available currency

questions.feedback_general: Per person means the total output divided by the population.

questions.text: A planner might say that modern computers solve the knowledge problem. How does the lesson treat that claim?

answers.text: It says economists disagree: some argue the problem is smaller now, while others argue the most useful knowledge is local, changing, and often unspoken

questions.feedback_general: The lesson asks you to be ready to defend whichever side you find stronger.

questions.text: How is the price of a Treasury security set when it is sold?

answers.text: By buyers and sellers, through public auctions where investors bid

questions.feedback_general: Households, banks, pension funds, and foreign investors all buy them.

questions.text: What does the phrase "ample reserves regime" in the Fed's 2020 announcement mean?

answers.text: The banking system holds so many reserves that the Fed steers rates with the interest it pays, not by limiting how many reserves exist

questions.feedback_general: The reserve requirement ratios were reduced to zero percent, effective March 26, 2020.

questions.text: What is amortization?

answers.text: Paying a loan off gradually in equal payments, each covering interest and also reducing the amount owed

questions.feedback_general: The payment stays the same, but the split between interest and principal changes every month.

questions.text: Which item does the lesson list as something credit scoring models look at?

answers.text: How much of your available credit you are using

questions.feedback_general: The Bureau's list includes your record of paying bills, how much debt you carry, how long accounts have been open, credit use, and recent applications.

questions.text: A family can refinance for $3,000 and cut its payment by $60 a month, but expects to move in three years. What does the break-even test suggest?

answers.text: Do not refinance, because 50 months are needed to earn back the cost and they will leave sooner

questions.feedback_general: $3,000 divided by $60 is 50 months. If you expect to move or pay off the loan sooner, you lose money by refinancing.
